noticias.texto:
The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.
My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.
Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’
One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.
Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.
The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.
The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.
For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.
The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’
The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.
But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.
Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.
Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.
Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.
Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
What else we’re reading about
Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.
Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.
Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
71
Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check
AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.
Get in touch
Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

noticias.titulo: Leaseholders in England and Wales to have ground rent capped in 2028
noticias.resumen: Housing minister hails ‘historic moment’ as he publishes bill to eventually ban almost all new leasehold properties Leaseholders in England and Wales will have their ground rent capped in 2028, the housing minister has said as he publishes a bill that will eventually ban virtually all new leasehold properties. Matthew Pennycook will introduce the government’s leasehold reform bill on Thursday, including measures to cap charges, end the sale of new leasehold flats and make it easier to extend and buy out leases. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Leaseholders in England and Wales will have their ground rent capped in 2028, the housing minister has said as he publishes a bill that will eventually ban virtually all new leasehold properties.
Matthew Pennycook will introduce the government’s leasehold reform bill on Thursday, including measures to cap charges, end the sale of new leasehold flats and make it easier to extend and buy out leases.
He said one of the first elements of the bill to come into force would be the long-promised £250 cap on annual ground rent – though it will not be enacted as quickly as some MPs have pushed for.
“The ground rent can be expected fairly early,” he said. “I think it will be a really historic moment … leasehold denies individuals control over the homes they live in and have paid for.
“It then allows freeholders and managing agents acting on their behalf to extract excessive amounts of money from them, whether that’s unreasonable or extortionate charges, punitive and escalating ground rents, unjustified administration and permission fees – you name it.
“Leasehold is an anachronism in the 21st century. I really do think that the bill that we’re introducing tomorrow [Thursday] marks the beginning of the end for the feudal leasehold system.”
Pennycook and his Conservative predecessors promised to end the leasehold system, which exists in only a few countries worldwide and dates back to feudal property laws.
Thursday’s bill will mark the biggest step towards making those promises a reality, extending the ban on leasehold for new houses to flats, which make up the bulk of leasehold properties. Pennycook has previously said he expects the ban to come into force after the next election.
It will also make it easier for those in leasehold properties to switch to a collective system known as commonhold, ensuring that such a move can be made with the agreement of half the residents in a block rather than all of them.
And it will end freeholders’ right to evict leaseholders for relatively small unpaid bills.
One of the first changes to become law will be the £250 cap on ground rent.
MPs on the housing select committee had urged Pennycook to introduce it as soon as next year, but he insisted it was not possible because of the “technical process” of beginning its enforcement. The 2028 date would not be explicitly included in the bill but ministers would enact it through secondary legislation, he said.
He also said many other leaseholders’ demands would have to come in a second law to be introduced later in the parliament.
They include establishing an independent regulator for property management agents and changing the rates that determine how much it costs to extend or buy out a lease.
Ministers are still considering proposals, meanwhile, which would strip out the costs of prospective future development from the cost of a lease.
Pennycook said that wrestling with the legal technicalities of property law had slowed the process of drafting the bill, arguing that doing so had minimised the risk of the government having to go back and rewrite parts of it.
“This is by far and away the most complex and technical piece of legislation I have ever dealt with,” he said.
“We are undertaking the most ambitious overhaul of land and property law in a century, if not longer … it is just ferociously complex.
“We’re taking on some big vested interests, and those vested interests have very deep pockets.
“Leasehold law is extremely litigious – we’ve had challenges brought to the 2024 Act … [and] we will get challenges to this piece of legislation as well, almost certainly.”

noticias.titulo: Member of anti-migrant group found guilty of Staffordshire murder
noticias.resumen: Raise the Colours activist Billy Allison, 36, killed man in ‘completely unprovoked and unjustified’ attack, say police A member of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours has been found guilty of murdering a man in a “completely unprovoked and unjustified” attack. Billy Allison, 36, delivered a “very, very hard” punch with the “stance and skill of an experienced fighter” which killed 44-year-old Matthew O’Gara while he was on a night out in Lichfield on 24 May. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A member of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours has been found guilty of murdering a man in a “completely unprovoked and unjustified” attack.
Billy Allison, 36, delivered a “very, very hard” punch with the “stance and skill of an experienced fighter” which killed 44-year-old Matthew O’Gara while he was on a night out in Lichfield on 24 May.
A jury of seven men and five women were not told of Allison’s link to Raise the Colours, which has been responsible for hanging hundreds of union jack flags on lamp-posts and roundabouts across the country, during the trial at Stafford crown court.
Allison was also found guilty of grievous bodily harm with intent on Wednesday for twice punching O’Gara’s friend, 62-year-old Adam Cooper, on the same night as the murder, leaving him with a fractured eye socket and nose.
O’Gara’s family thanked the emergency services who cared for him and said he remained “deeply loved” and “will always hold a special place in our hearts”.
“While the conclusion of the court proceedings has brought a measure of justice, it can never replace the loss we have suffered or bring Matthew back,” they said in a statement.
The trial heard how Allison had been drinking and had taken cocaine before he attacked the two men – neither of whom he knew.
He had spent the day with his partner, Charlotte Dean, and fellow Raise the Colours members Ryan Bridge and Ben Cullen and their partners.
CCTV images capturing the lead-up to the assault showed Allison in the corner of the dancefloor alongside Bridge at about 11.30pm.
Prosecution counsel Timothy Hannam described how Allison, without warning, then took three “purposeful” steps toward an “oblivious” O’Gara and delivered a “very, very hard punch” causing him to fall to the floor and become “motionless”.
The punch was “hard enough to break several bones” in O’Gara’s neck, Hannam said, and caused a massive brain haemorrhage which resulted in the 44-year-old going into cardiac arrest. He died in hospital two days later.
Allison, who had participated in and won boxing competitions, then delivered two “powerful boxer punches” to Cooper’s face. “In total, three devastating punches had been delivered in about six seconds,” Hannam said, adding that the two men had been “demolished by them”.
O’Gara’s partner, Rebecca Mullally, gave evidence during the trial and said O’Gara and their friends were in a “good mood” before the assault.
She said she heard Allison’s punch because it was “really loud” and she did not see “anybody provoke anyone” before the attack.
“I‘ve never seen a punch like that before,” she said. “I did think: ‘Has that killed him?’ It was hard.”
Cooper also gave evidence during the trial and said he felt an “almighty blow to my face” when he was punched by Allison, likening it to a “sledgehammer”.
“I didn’t know it was coming [and] I made no attempt to defend myself,” he said, before describing how blood then poured out of his face.
After the attack, Allison fled the bar via a back entrance with Cullen and the pair swapped T-shirts. Allison was later found by police at the Cathedral Hotel in Beacon Street at 5am, where Cullen had booked to stay the night. He later answered “no comment” during police questioning.
Police body-worn camera footage showed Allison being told his victim had died and he was facing a murder charge. Allison could be heard muttering “fuck” and “fuck’s sake”.
In his evidence to the court, Allison said he was “really sorry” for what he had done and “really sorry my actions caused the end of someone’s life”.
He said he had never intended to cause anyone really serious injury or death, but accepted O’Gara and Cooper had not done anything to provoke the attack.
Allison added: “I just don’t have an explanation for why … I had a bit of a sense I was being looked at, in my drunken state, maybe I was a touch paranoid.
“I didn’t intentionally punch him that hard.”
DI Lisa Holland, who led the investigation, said: “Matthew O’Gara’s family have been left devastated by his death and our thoughts remain firmly with them.
“This was a wholly unprovoked attack carried out by Allison on a man he did not know and who posed no threat to him. In a matter of seconds, Allison’s actions changed the lives of Matthew’s loved ones for ever.
“The evidence in this case showed that Allison approached Matthew without warning and struck him, causing catastrophic injuries from which he never recovered. He then went on to seriously assault another man.”
Allison, who is facing a mandatory life sentence, has been remanded ahead of his sentencing at Stafford crown court on 5 January.

noticias.titulo: Birmingham council granted interim ban on union jacks on lamp-posts
noticias.resumen: High court judge issues order against Raise the Colours over flags on council-owned street furniture The campaign group Raise the Colours has been temporarily banned from placing union jacks on lamp-posts and roundabouts in Birmingham after a legal challenge by the local council. The high court judge Emma Kelly granted an interim injunction banning the placing of all flags on council-owned street furniture without prior permission in a judgment issued on Wednesday, Birmingham city council said. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The campaign group Raise the Colours has been temporarily banned from placing union jacks on lamp-posts and roundabouts in Birmingham after a legal challenge by the local council.
The high court judge Emma Kelly granted an interim injunction banning the placing of all flags on council-owned street furniture without prior permission in a judgment issued on Wednesday, Birmingham city council said.
The council, run by a minority coalition led by the Liberal Democrats, sought the injunction against seven people identified as supporting or participating in the affixing of flags in the city, including Ryan Bridge, a co-founder of Raise the Colours, and “persons unknown”.
The application for an injunction, which attracted national attention and follows similar action by Oxfordshire county council, argued the actions of the flag activists had caused danger, alarm and distress.
People associated with Raise the Colours, which describes itself as a grassroots movement, have been placing union jacks and St George’s flags on public infrastructure across the country since August last year.
The group’s website states it is a “campaign to cover Britain in symbols of unity and patriotism”. However, others have accused the group of racism and spreading anti-immigration rhetoric – claims it has previously denied.
In its claim to the high court, Birmingham city council said the defendants had travelled across the city “unlawfully affixing flags” and had confronted residents who attempted to remove them.
“In doing so, they are engaging in tortious and criminal behaviour, which is both antisocial and dangerous,” the claim read, adding that the behaviour had caused “danger” and “alarm” to residents.
The council said residents of Birmingham had suffered “fear, anxiety, intimidation, harassment,” been put at “serious risk of harm”, and some had suffered physical injuries, including a broken leg.
The case was adjourned in early September after the judge said she was “troubled by the lack of clarity” from the council “against the individual defendants”, and a further hearing was scheduled at the end of September.
Bridge opposed the injunction and read a written statement to the court. He said: “For me, the union flag represents home, identity, belonging, national identity, British culture and patriotism.”
His lawyer, Liam Wells, argued that the injunction would have a “chilling effect” on human rights and that erecting union jacks and St George’s flags was an expression of his political views.
Wells said the interim injunction would risk “silencing people in their political views and expression of political opinions” and the council had failed to prove Bridge had acted unlawfully.
Three local residents, Adam Biggs, Mark Hudson and Tony Kaye, joined the case representing ‘persons unknown’ opposing the injunction bid, and expressed concerns it would ban people flying flags for pride and other campaigns.
The council’s cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, said on Wednesday the local authority was grateful for the judgment and it was an “important step”.
“We have taken a proportionate and evidence-led approach throughout this case. Our priority has always been to protect public safety, supporting the welfare of our staff and contractors, maintaining community cohesion and ensuring public funds are used responsibly,” she said.
In a video uploaded to Facebook, Bridge said he was “gutted” and “devastated” by the decision, including the fact that the injunction granted power of arrest against him and others.
He said Raise the Colours was “not about race, colour, creed” but about opposing “illegal invaders breaking in our country, jeopardising our borders, on the rubber dinghies”.
At the Reform UK conference in Birmingham in September, Nigel Farage promised to help Bridge in his legal fight if the party was able to do so.
In response to the judgment, Reform’s leader in Birmingham, Jex Parkin, said the council had its “priorities entirely wrong” and had pursued an “ideologically driven case against residents proudly displaying our national flags – at huge public expense”.
The leader of the local Conservatives, Robert Alden, also criticised the injunction and said the council was “punishing ordinary Birmingham residents who simply want to show pride in where they live”.
He said: “Amidst a 23-month bin strike, loss of roads funding, and mounting litter on our streets, the council has chosen to make this court action a priority.”
The group Brummies United Against Racism, which campaigned for the injunction, welcomed the judgment. Members of the group told the Guardian earlier this year they had presented evidence of incidents involving Raise the Colours to the police and council officers.
The group said it was “not opposed to this country’s flag” and many of its supporters “see the flag as a symbol of celebration and unity”. “However, we are firmly opposed to those who seek to use the flag to further an agenda of hate and who dress up racism as patriotism,” a statement read.
A further hearing in the case will take place on Thursday.
Additional reporting by PA

noticias.titulo: Elon Musk claims ‘I’m not Maga’ and says he regrets vast sums to back Republicans
noticias.resumen: Musk, who aligned with Trump and was frequent White House guest, says he feels ‘pretty foolish’ about record midterm spending Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intensely with Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement since 2024. “I’m not Maga,” the world’s richest person told the New York Times Dealbook summit, which he attended via video call from China, where he is one of several US business leaders who have accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intensely with Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement since 2024.
“I’m not Maga,” the world’s richest person told the New York Times Dealbook summit, which he attended via video call from China, where he is one of several US business leaders who have accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia.
“I’m not sure what Maga means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that,” the chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla added.
Musk famously declared at a 2024 campaign rally in Madison Square Garden: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.”
In a 45-minute interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin, a New York Times columnist, Musk also said it would be good for Washington to have split control between the two parties, and that he thinks “there are positives and negatives in both”.
He also accused Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, of “lying” about restrictions on access to his firm’s Starshield satellite system; praised Jensen Huang, the ousted Nvidia chief executive; and said that “no one I met at Anthropic set off my evil detector”.
Asked about his previous negative comments about Anthropic, Musk said that before he agreed to rent computing power to the AI firm: “I went to met with a lot of people at Anthropic. I didn’t just move forward with the deal.”
“My interaction so far with the Anthropic team is that they seem like good people and they seem principled,” Musk added. “They seem diligent and they seem seem to care about the future.”
Musk donated at least $250m of his own money to help Trump win the election in 2024, and recently spent nearly $500m in the US midterms to support Republicans, many of whom lost.
Musk admitted at the Dealbook summit that his spending had “failed”, and that he felt “pretty foolish” for spending such a sum, the most that anyone has ever spent in a political cycle when they themselves did not run for office. “It certainly shows that American elections are not just about money,” he said. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”
After Trump took office for the second time in 2025, Musk served for 180 days heading the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) within Trump’s administration, before stepping down following a very public falling out with the president.
That culminated in Musk posting on his social media platform in June of that year: “Time to drop the really big bomb: @realDonaldTrump is in the Epstein files. That is the real reason they have not been made public.”
The two men later reconciled. During his time leading Doge, Musk frequently appeared in the Oval Office and at cabinet meetings alongside the president, often sporting hats that read “Make America Great Again” or “Trump was right about everything”.

noticias.titulo: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from freeways across the US after California ban

noticias.texto:
Waymo has stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways across the US indefinitely. The Alphabet subsidiary pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after California banned them from freeways in response to recent traffic incidents.
Waymo had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas, including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver. Those rides remain unaffected by suspended freeway service.
A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”. The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn’t say how long it would last.
Waymo’s voluntary suspension came the same day as the California department of motor vehicles banned the company’s robotaxis from the state’s freeways. The ban followed two traffic incidents, including one in which three Waymo driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, a DMV spokesperson, Jonathan Groveman, said in a statement.
The construction zone incident occurred on 5 November, and the second incident, which involved California highway patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.
Video of the 6 November incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.
“The department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on 18 May.
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions”.
California’s restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on the state’s freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions”.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic sets share price at $83 for stock market debut, above expected range
noticias.resumen: Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange. The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set it
noticias.texto:
Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange.
The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX.
Amodei is planning to sell about $260m worth of shares with the IPO, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range, the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each.
When Anthropic filed for its IPO last month, the company detailed rapidly rising revenue in its prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.
Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.
Anthropic’s main expenditure listed in its investor prospectus is computing power from datacenters. The company has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.
Anthropic is the first company at the forefront of the generative AI boom to go public, and its performance is likely to affect investors’ enthusiasm. Its competitor OpenAI was slated to hit Wall Street later this year, but CEO Sam Altman has said that the company opted to delay its IPO until it can overcome safety concerns.
Anthropic’s IPO comes during a volatile time for AI and the stock market. Last month, the industry saw a broader slowdown, with share prices dropping at several companies amid growing concern about the technology. Then, last week, Nvidia, which designs the chips AI companies use to power their chatbots, was racked with a scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang resigning after reports of multiple extramarital affairs.

noticias.titulo: Almost 1 in 4 children live in conflict zones — report
noticias.resumen: Denial of humanitarian access, abductions and sexual violence are among several violations against children that have increased dramtically over the past year, according to a new report by Save the Children.
noticias.texto:
Almost 1 in 4 children live in conflict zones — report
November 19, 2026
A record number of children were living in a conflict zone in 2025, Save the Children findings revealed on Thursday.
In the latest report in the "Stop the War on Children" series, the humantarian group said 589 million children worldwide lived in conflict zones. That's the highest number since records began in 1990, and more than double the total in the mid-1990s.
"For millions of children, fear, violence and displacement are part of every day life," said Save the Children Germany CEO Florian Westphal.
He said this needed to be a "wake-up call" for the international community.
Where children are living in conflict zones
Around two in five children in both Africa and the Middle East were living in conflict zones in 2025, the report found. Africa, alone, accounted for 44% of all children living in conflict zones worldwide.
In terms of regional proportions, 40.2% of children in the Middle East were living in conflict zones in 2025. That represented roughly two in five children across the region, and a particularly steep rise in the number of children affected. The figure jumped by nearly 29% from 52 million in 2024 to 67 million last year.
Children's exposure to conflict in Africa has more than tripled over the past 15 years, with the share of children living in conflict zones rising from 12% in 2010 to 39% in 2025.
Grave violations against children in armed conflict zones increase
The report highlighted the dramatic increase in the denial of humanitarian access.
A total of 8,322 verified incidents of denying access to humanitarian aid to children were recorded in 2025, a 16-fold rise over the past decade. The figure was 509 in 2015, and only eight incidents were reported when the United Nations (UN) established the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM) in 2005.
The Palestinian Territories accounted for the vast majority of cases, with 5,946 incidents, or more than 70% of all verified cases globally.
"No grave violation has increased as dramatically or changed the overall pattern of verified violations as much as the denial of humanitarian access," the study noted.
According to the report, denial of humanitarian access rose from around 2% of all verified grave violations against children in 2015 to more than 21% in 2025, becoming the second-most frequently recorded violation after the killing and maiming of children.
Grave violations as laid out in the MRM also include the recruitment of children by armed forces, sexual violence, abduction and attacks on schools and hospitals.
Where violations against children were concentrated
The study found that, overall, 38,967 grave violations against children were verified by the UN.
This was the second-highest annual total since the MRM was established, surpassed only by the record 41,763 violations documented in 2024.
More than half of these took place in just three areas: the Palestinian Territories, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria. The Palestinian Territories alone accounted for 12,449 verified violations, nearly one-third of all cases.
As well as the denial of humanitarian access, violations in 2025 included:
- 14,224 children killed or maimed in conflicts in 2025
- A record 5,128 child abductions
- 1,787 cases of sexual violence, a 71% increase in the past decade
- A fifth straight year of increased attacks on schools and hospitals, at 2,930 cases
The Palestinian Territories recorded the highest number of attacks on schools or hospitals, with 837 incidents, followed by Ukraine with 643. Together, the two accounted for more than half of all reported cases worldwide.
The sharpest rises in sexual violence incidents were recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where cases jumped from 358 in 2024 to 592 in 2025, and Sudan, which saw an increase from 74 to 193. Around 86% of all cases were documented in African conflict zones.
"Children have the right to live free from violence. Changing the odds requires political choices that put children’s safety first, and a sustained commitment to stop the war on children," the NGO said.

noticias.titulo: Grand Theft Auto VI released as gamers rejoice globally
noticias.resumen: After 13 years of waiting, fans around the world will get to play the latest installment in the blockbuster video game series. In focus: A tale of crime and violence in a fictionalized version of Miami.
noticias.texto:
Grand Theft Auto VI released as gamers rejoice globally
November 19, 2026
Grand Theft Auto VI will be officially launched Thursday, ending a 13-year wait for one of the most anticipated games ever.
The game will become playable at midnight local time (CET) on a wide range of platforms, including PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, meaning gamers in Asia will get to play the game ahead of users in the US and Europe.
In New Zealand, one of the first countries worldwide where the game became available, the release prompted internet providers to prepare for a spike in internet usage at midnight.
This comes due to the game's size of 212 gigabytes, more than a quarter of the average New Zealand household's usage in a month.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA franchise, faces high expectation after 13 years of anticipation, with previous versions having become commercial and cultural hits around the world.
GTA games sold 470 million units worldwide, and the fifth installment generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days after its release in 2013.
GTA's global success
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar Games' parent company, saw its shares rise by more than eight percent the day before the game's release.
The game takes place in Vice City, a fictional version of Miami.
It follows Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple drawn into criminal networks while trying to secure a better life. GTA games are often criticized for including excessive violence and for glorifying crimes and drug use.
Lucia, a former prisoner, and Jason, an ex-military man, experience a series of criminal jobs that go wrong in the drug-trafficking world of Leonida, a fictional state based on Florida.
According to Rockstar, Leonida is the company's most detailed open world so far, extending beyond Vice City into smaller communities and nightlife hotspots inspired by locations in South Florida.
Music has been an intrinsic part of the GTA experience, and the latest game is expected to feature a soundtrack including artists like Tame Impala and SZA.

noticias.titulo: What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
noticias.resumen: When "GTA VI" is released on November 19, millions of people worldwide will rush to their consoles to play it. How has this video game created such a cross-generational buzz?
noticias.texto:
What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
November 18, 2026
"Oh, it's so on now!" is the tagline in the latest trailer for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI" for short.
"GTA VI" is a game of superlatives that's been crashing through records. The hype around it is unparalleled. No game in history has clocked so many pre-orders. It's thought that around 10 million people have already purchased it. There's no denying it: "GTA VI" is a global cultural phenomenon.
A few days before its release on November 19, fans can already start downloading the game. The file is so large that downloading it can take several days, depending on the internet connection. Providers have already registered a significant spike in data traffic.
As soon as the game is unlocked, players can start speeding through the fictional US metropolis of Vice City in a stylish sports car with criminal couple Jason and Lucia.
Miami gets cast as Vice City
To mark the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," its real-life inspiration — Miami — is getting a full-scale "Vice City" makeover. This promotional push includes the Miami Heat basketball team stepping onto the hardwood in custom "Vice City" jerseys for a home game, a local festival featuring artists from the game's official soundtrack, and roadside "Vice City" signage installed across the area.
Expectations for "GTA VI" are sky-high. Nearly 5,000 people have been working on the game for more than 10 years. Development costs are estimated at around $1 billion (€900 million).
"Based on those figures alone — as well as the series' extremely successful and popular track record — this can certainly be described as a truly exceptional release," says Rudolf Thomas Inderst, cultural studies scholar and professor of Game Design and Game Studies at Germany's Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences.
When such an effort is put into a product, it's only natural for people to expect great things, he adds. Inderst is expecting "GTA VI" to showcase the absolute best of what modern gaming can do across gameplay, storytelling, visuals and tech.
Social satire and gameplay freedom
This video game series has been around for almost three decades, setting new standards through its different versions. A biting satire on US society and the American dream, "GTA" parodies politics, culture and the media.
The game is also renowned for its gameplay freedom and spectacularly staged chaos in a crazy world where players can do whatever they please. Shoot down helicopters with a bazooka, go to the hairdresser's, take a stroll on the beach, go to a nightclub, take part in car races and much more.
What makes it a standout among video games is how its NPCs — non-player characters, those not being controlled by a human player — are brought to life. They respond based on a player's interactions with them, displaying individualized behaviors and traits ranging from fear to hostility. "GTA VI" has an estimated 600,000 animations for the civilians in the fictional state of Leonida.
'Grand Theft Auto,' a long-running hit
"GTA VI" is essentially a huge adult playground, striking a chord across several generations. Millennials grew up with "Grand Theft Auto III," "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City," "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas," and "Grand Theft Auto IV," while Gen Z grew up with "Grand Theft Auto V." Generation Alpha might still be too young for the latest edition, but will likely find ways to play it anyway.
Social media has certainly played a part in the series' ongoing success, particularly "GTA V" and its multiplayer spin-off, "GTA Online." Numerous content creators stream gameplay sessions on Twitch or YouTube, and particularly funny or crazy gameplay moments end up on TikTok.
At the same time, a dedicated role-play community has grown around the game. Players gather inside the world of "GTA" to act out specific characters, such as taxi drivers, judges or small-time criminals. They invent realistic backstories for their personas, and many even use accents to stay in character.
Perfectionism has its downsides
The hype surrounding "GTA VI" is not only good news for the game itself but could also boost the entire games industry by drawing more people back to their consoles. This is because the boom triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic was followed by studio closures and redundancies. Worldwide, it's estimated that 50,000 people in the games industry have lost their jobs since 2022.
But while publisher Rockstar Games is well-known for the meticulous polish of its titles and attention to detail, the perfectionism so prized by fans also has its drawbacks, especially for those working on the game. Rockstar, like many other game developers, has frequently faced major criticism regarding its labor practices.
Former developers report extremely long working hours and a heavy workload that resulted in health issues. Trade unions accuse company managers of employee surveillance, resulting in a culture of workplace stress and low morale.
Coinciding with the launch of Rockstar's largest game to date, the developers behind it are pushing for trade union recognition. That move would give them a collective voice to address working hours, pay, pensions and parental leave. If successful, their campaign could set a major precedent for the wider video game industry, which continues to face challenges around fair labor practices.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: APEC summit: Xi, Trump and Putin to hold first-ever trilateral in China
noticias.resumen: Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin are scheduled to sit down for a three-way summit today. Follow live.
noticias.texto:
APEC summit: Xi, Trump and Putin to hold historic trilateral in China
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- A widely anticipated meeting of presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will last an hour or less on Thursday, according to the Kremlin
- Trump and Putin have shaken hands for the first time in more than a year ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit
- Trump was greeted by Xi at the airport earlier on Wednesday
Here are the biggest headlines from Trump's Asia tour on Wednesday, November 18:
Welcome back to our coverage on Thursday
President Donald Trump is set for a historic meeting with Presidents Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit today.
Xi traveled to the airport on Wednesday to personally greet Trump on arrival in a rare signal of diplomatic respect.
Putin also approached Trump before fellow leaders got into position for the traditional summit family photo.
The two shook hands, while Xi looked on.
A bilateral summit between Trump and Putin might not come to pass while both are in China.
We'll have the latest out of the summit in this blog, thank you for joining.
Trump's Asia trip: What happened in China on Wednesday and what is expected on Thursday
US President Donald Trump landed in Shenzhen, China on Wednesday for the APEC summit, and was embraced by Chinese President Xi Jinping upon arrival.
Xi told Trump after his arrival that he looked forward to "an in-depth exchange views" with the US president "with the aim of advancing a constructive, strategically stable relationship between our two nations — one built upon the foundations of mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity."
Trump also shook hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in their first face-to-face meeting since the 2025 Alaska summit.
The US president spoke with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on the sidelines of the APEC event amid trade tensions.
On Thursday, Trump, Xi and Putin are expected to hold trilateral talks, with the Kremlin saying these talks will last for "no more than an hour."
Trump and Putin are also expected to hold a separate bilateral meeting as Russia's invasion of Ukraine continues.
It's still unclear if North Korean leader Kim Jong Un could make a guest appearance on Thursday at the APEC summit.
Trump and Putin to hold bilateral talks in addition to trilateral meet with Xi
Kremlin and White House sources on Wednesday said Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet with US President Donald Trump on Thursday before the two hold trilateral talks with Chinese host, President Xi Jinping.
Russian state media quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying the two would not hold full-scale negotiations on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen despite global urgency for Putin to end his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which is approaching its fifth year.
The White House offered no information beyond confirming that talks would take place.
Russian media cited foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov saying that the Putin-Trump meeting would include Russian and US delegations and follow an APEC plenary session.
What could come of denuclearization talks?
Donald Trump says he wants to discuss "denuclearization" with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. But White House officials, briefing media ahead of the meeting, sought to downplay expectations. China has long rejected talks on limiting its nuclear arsenal, pointing out that the US and Russia have far more warheads than it has and that if any cuts could be made, they should be the ones to make them.
But nuclear might is more than just counting warheads. China is ahead of the US in the crucial field of theater nukes. Beijing has developed advanced, precision missiles that could prove decisive in a potential war over Taiwan. Here, far from denuclearizing, the US is racing to catch up — with multiple new missiles in development.
So what could emerge from Trump's push to talk about nuclear weapons with Putin and Xi? There might be more scope for progress in what is called "risk reduction," such as a trilateral agreement to notify each other of missile test launches or joint commitments on the role of AI in nuclear command and control systems. Trump's predecessor, Joe Biden, and Xi agreed to an initial statement that humans, not AI, should make decisions on nuclear weapons use.
Short of that, the three leaders could again affirm the Reagan-Gorbachev mantra that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought."
But beware of reading too much into such a statement — the last time they did so, Putin invaded Ukraine seven weeks later.
Xi-Putin-Trump meeting to take an hour or less, Kremlin says
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin is not expected to last longer than an hour, that's according to the Kremlin spokesperson quoted by Russian media.
"No more than an hour" has been set aside for the summit between the trio, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media.
Russian officials also said that no "full-scale" talks directly between Trump and Putin were planned for Thursday, and that their handshake and meeting on Wednesday did not amount to a "substantive conversation."
Although the planned trilateral meeting has prompted some comparisons to the 1945 Yalta conference that helped define the settlement at the end of World War II and set the stage for the coming Cold War, this detail underlined one of the many differences that should be apparent even at first glance.
Yalta followed years of close cooperation between war allies on political as well as military levels, and then involved eight days of intense negotiations, rather than occurring during a larger, long-planned summit and lasting roughly as long as it takes to eat a meal.
Sheinbaum's economy flight impresses in China
Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum won praise on Chinese social media for her frugal travel plans this week, taking an economy flight to Shenzhen.
The Mexican president took a South China Airlines flight from Mexico City to Shenzhen, with posts going viral on China's Weibo social media site seemingly showing Sheinbaum chatting with other passengers on board.
She posted a short video on social media showing her being greeted by Chinese officials and schoolchildren after getting off an airport bus, as well as an earlier post showing her waiting in Mexico City's airport departures lounge.
A hashtag on Weibo about her arrival attracted more than 10 million views, with users voicing admiration for her low-cost intercontinental travel.
"It's commendable to spend taxpayer money frugally and ensure it's used where it's most needed, rather than squandering it on luxurious private jets or official travel expenses," the AFP news agency cited one user as saying.
Sheinbaum is promoting an austerity program launched by her predecessor, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who put the Mexican presidential plane up for sale in 2023.
She traveled with a large delegation of ministers to Shenzhen.
China has become particularly sensitive to the idea of corruption and wasteful public spending in recent years amid high-profile and long-running anti-corruption measures launched by President Xi Jinping, seemingly at least partly as damage-limitation efforts following a series of scandals.
Canada's Carney, Mexico's Sheinbaum hold talks with Trump
The leaders of Canada and Mexico have both reported on separate meetings with the US president on the sidelines of the APEC summit, amid difficult trade talks with the main economic power in the Americas.
"The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada's languages, culture, and sovereignty," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's office said. "They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact."
Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum published a photo of her "very good meeting with President Donald Trump and his team" online, saying "we continue to make progress on our shared agenda."
Trump, Putin shake hands in first face-to-face encounter since Alaska summit
The presidents of the US and Russia have shaken hands in their first in-person meeting since August 2025, when Putin was invited to Alaska for talks primarily concerning Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin shook hands in the presence of host Xi Jinping ahead of the leaders' welcome banquet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
The encounter follows a rare sign of progress in the US-led efforts to broker an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine, a conflict Trump repeatedly claimed he would settle in "a day" if reelected.
The two are expected to have a private meeting on Thursday.
Talks took place last week in Abu Dhabi involving Russia, Ukraine and European representatives, with Trump's negotiating team subsequently traveling to the Kremlin for a meeting with Putin and other Russian officials.
WATCH: Xi greets Trump at the airport
Trump's arrival was highly choreographed: He descended from Air Force One and stood on a red carpet lined with people waving colorful pom poms. Trump and Xi hugged before shaking hands.
Potential Trump talks touted in Shenzhen, even with Kim Jong Un
The White House, other countries and Donald Trump himself have all listed possible or probable bilateral or multilateral talks involving the US president on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, beyond Thursday's highly-anticipated US-China-Russia meeting.
Some of the more notable examples are listed here:
- Kremlin officials said they expected a meeting between just Trump and Putin, but not one long or substantial enough for fully-fledged bilateral negotiations
- The White House said Trump would hold two separate meetings with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum prior to the official APEC greeting ceremony
- While in Manila, Trump himself floated the possibility of a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jong Un, but without voicing a solid intent
- China said it had no information on a potential Trump-Kim meeting
- Meanwhile, North Korean state media — which typically operates behind the global news cycle — has only released images of Kim visiting a ski resort and Mount Paektu, making no mention of possible Shenzhen travel plans
Xi tells Trump China seeks 'strategically stable relationship'
Chinese news agency Xinhua has reported the first comments from Xi Jinping to Donald Trump following his arrival.
"I look forward to an in-depth exchange of views with you on major issues concerning China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the global landscape," Xi told Trump.
He said the talks would take place "with the aim of advancing a constructive, strategically stable relationship between our two nations — one built upon the foundations of mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity."
Despite Trump and Xi's efforts to regularly hold friendly face-to-face talks in recent months, the US and China are nevertheless embroiled in difficult trade negotiations as the two superpowers try to reconcile competing interests on various issues.
The two sides have been periodically extending a temporary tariff truce designed to bridge the gap until they can reach a more permanent agreement, which for now has proven elusive. China announced the most recent extension earlier this month, to run until early January.
Nvidia stops shipping US-approved chips to China
The interim CEO of US chip giant Nvidia says the company is not currently shipping Hopper-generation data center products to China.
These are some of the most advanced Nvidia products licensed for export by the US government; the company had sold such goods worth $2.4 billion (roughly €2.2 billion) in the previous quarter, Colette Kress said.
Kress replaced Jensen Huang following his resignation last week and amid the scandal over alleged Chinese attempts both to gain intelligence on the company's CEO and to circumvent import restrictions.
"Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," Kress said.
She did not specify why such deliveries had currently stopped or say whether the step would be permanent.
Huang was influential in persuading Donald Trump to allow sales of H200 Hopper processors used to train and run advanced AI models to China, reversing export controls the US had imposed in 2022 under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.
China has called the allegations of espionage targeting Nvidia unfounded and threatened to respond in kind if restrictions on trade follow as a result of the fallout from Huang's resignation.
Donald Trump arrives at Shenzhen Airport ahead of summit
US President Donald Trump has landed at Shenzhen Airport on Air Force One and disembarked.
He left Manila in the Philippines a few hours earlier.
Trump will be attending the APEC summit but is also expected to take part in a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
Xi greeted Trump at the airport on Wednesday, mirroring a gesture Trump had recently extended during the Chinese leader's state visit to the US in September.
Japan's Sanae Takaichi on first China trip since becoming PM
Sanae Takaichi arrived in China for the APEC summit, which is also her first official visit to the country as Japanese prime minister.
Takaichi's moves to bolster Japan's military and comments last year on Taiwan have upset Beijing and severely affected bilateral ties.
In particular, Takaichi's suggestion that Tokyo could intervene militarily if Beijing sought to forcibly take Taiwan — which China considers its territory — led to friction between the regional rivals with a troubled 20th century history and ongoing territorial disputes.
China imposed trade restrictions and urged citizens not to travel to Japan, which had become an increasingly popular tourist destination. Traffic is down by roughly half this year as a result.
A formal one-on-one meeting between Takaichi and China's Xi Jinping is considered highly unlikely, but Japan's NHK public broadcaster did report that Xi would "personally greet her" before Wednesday's banquet.
IN DEPTH: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
Read DW's full report on what Trump, Xi and Putin are hoping to extract from the trilateral talks.

noticias.titulo: Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
noticias.resumen: The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.
noticias.texto:
Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
November 17, 2026
During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.
Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.
What does Russia mean by 1997?
The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.
According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.
What would be the consequences of a NATO withdrawal?
A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.
In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.
"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."
The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.
Why isn't the mutual-defense clause enough?
In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.
For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.
Who decides which alliances a country can join?
As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.
Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.
Was there a promise not to expand NATO eastward?
During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.
Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.
In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.
In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.
Why is the demand back on the table?
Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.
Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.
So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.
This article was originally published in German.

noticias.titulo: Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay
noticias.resumen: The European Court of Human Rights has called for the release of imprisoned elected lawmaker Can Atalay. Atalay has been in prison for almost five years despite rulings from the Turkish Constitutional Court.
noticias.texto:
Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay
November 17, 2026
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.
The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.
The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.
It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.
The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.
Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.
From leading activist to a jailed member of parliament
As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.
He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.
Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup."
Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.
A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.
His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.
Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.
After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

noticias.titulo: Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
noticias.resumen: Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.
noticias.texto:
Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
November 17, 2026
Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.
This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.
The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month.
Since Huang's resignation, some investors — including Elon Musk and Donald Trump — have voiced concern that his departure could leave Nvidia and America's AI sector in peril and are now calling for his return. Huang on Tuesday, expressed regret for "serious mistakes" in his personal life before declaring he would be "honored" to return if the company's board of directors thought that was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."
What are Nvidia's plans for the new oversight committee?
Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.
Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).
The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.
Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.
"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.
The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.
The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month. 
How has the scandal highlighted the question of US-China chip trade?
US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.
"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."
Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.
Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.
That company, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.
The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

noticias.titulo: Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens
noticias.resumen: Serbia's Student List's candidates have taken their oaths in the inaugural parliament session. As the new majority, they have 90 days to form a government.
noticias.texto:
Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens
November 17, 2026
Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.
The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government.
The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.
Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade, to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.
Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.
According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.
90 days to form a government
The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.
The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.
They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.
The election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.
A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.
Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.

noticias.titulo: Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future
noticias.resumen: Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.
noticias.texto:
Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future
November 17, 2026
"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.
Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.
