noticias.titulo: Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh and south
noticias.resumen: Material damage was reported after ​debris fell following the latest Houthi strikes launched towards Saudi Arabia.
noticias.texto:
Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh and south
Material damage was reported after debris fell following the latest Houthi strikes launched towards Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis says it has intercepted missiles fired towards Riyadh and Saudi Arabia’s southern region after a loud boom was heard in the capital.
The attacks on Thursday are the latest in weeks of strikes by the Yemeni armed group targeting Saudi military, civilian and oil infrastructure.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said on X that its forces “dealt with” a Houthi missile threat launched towards Riyadh.
An initial assessment showed debris had fallen and that material damage had been reported, he added, saying the extent of the damage was still being determined.
Hours later, in a separate post, the spokesman said air defences intercepted and destroyed four ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), towards the southern region, bordering Yemen.
The coalition said it had earlier also destroyed a ballistic missile launchpad used in the attempted attacks on Riyadh.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for targeting vital sites in the Saudi capital on Thursday, including the international airport and the financial centre, as well as Khamis Mushait and Abha city in the south, where alerts were sounded.
A Saudi aircraft, meanwhile, carried out air raids on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, Sanaa, earlier on Thursday, the group-run Saba news agency reported, without providing further details.
The latest attacks in Saudi Arabia coincided with an announcement by Yemeni government forces that they carried out about 750 air strikes and operations against the Houthis on several fronts, including in Taiz and Lahij, where the humanitarian situation is worsening day by day.
Earlier on Thursday, the United Nations children’s agency, UNICEF, said in a statement that “more than 330,000 people, including an estimated 174,000 children, have been displaced since the beginning of the renewed military escalations”.
“The number of casualties is likely to increase as renewed fighting continues around densely populated areas, particularly in Taiz” and Lahij, UNICEF said.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council issued a decision designating the Houthi group a “terrorist” organisation on Thursday. It said anyone who cooperates with the group will face prosecution and punishment, with penalties that could include execution or prison terms of 30 years or more, Al Jazeera’s Yasser Hassan reported from Taiz.
Humanitarian organisations have released new figures on the casualties in the war, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has intensified since the group captured strategic areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month.
The World Health Organization said this week that the death toll from the latest escalation that began in August has reached 2,260, with 10,519 wounded.
The renewed conflict between the two sides has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted the exchange of attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the most populous parts of the country.

noticias.titulo: Why is Pete Hegseth strengthening US military ties with Venezuela?
noticias.resumen: Hegseth's new military deal with Venezuela raises questions about US influence, regional security and Maduro's removal.
noticias.texto:
Why is Pete Hegseth strengthening US military ties with Venezuela?
Hegseth’s new military deal with Venezuela raises questions about US influence, regional security and Maduro’s removal.
Hegseth unveils new US-Venezuela military deal
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a new cooperation agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooperation between the two countries.
The Pentagon chief’s announcement came during an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday. The US says the agreement will help fight drug trafficking and improve security in the region. Venezuela says it will help strengthen its military without compromising its sovereignty.
But why is an agreement happening now, and what does each side stand to gain?
Here is what we know:
What is the new US-Venezuela military agreement?
The US and Venezuela have agreed to strengthen military cooperation in several areas, including joint training, intelligence sharing, military equipment and border security.
Hegseth met Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez and Defence Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez in Caracas. He said the agreement would allow the two countries’ armed forces to work together to combat drug trafficking and armed groups operating in Venezuela.
Rodriguez described Hegseth’s visit as an extraordinary step in relations between the two countries.
She said renewed military cooperation would help improve troop training, modernise equipment and give armed forces access to new technologies.
Her government said the country’s armed forces, known as the Bolivarian National Armed Forces (FANB), would benefit directly from the agreement.
However, the full terms of the agreement have not been made public, including details of how the two countries would carry out joint military operations.
Why is the US strengthening military ties with Venezuela?
The Trump administration said closer military cooperation with Venezuela will help fight drug trafficking and armed groups, and improve security in the region.
Hegseth said the agreement should help Venezuela regain control of areas where armed groups and drug trafficking networks operate.
But political analyst Carlos Pina said the timing of the visit is important, particularly after the Democrats won the midterm elections in the US.
“I think many of the things happening between the United States and Venezuela are closely related to the November 3 election results,” Pina said.
He explained that the Democrats have already said they aim to increase scrutiny of US foreign policy towards Venezuela, including the agreements reached with Caracas during 2026, after US forces abducted then-President Nicolas Maduro and took him to New York. The US has since, in effect, taken control of Venezuela’s oil industry — the country has the world’s largest oil reserves.
Pina also pointed out the recent attempt to impeach Hegseth. “I think this Hegseth visit also falls within that framework, to get ahead of what will be the debate in the new US Congress.”
On November 10, the House of Representatives voted 211-204 against impeaching Hegseth for now, but Democrats could try again after January, with their new majority in the House.
The November resolution against Hegseth, introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, included eight articles of impeachment related to the US-Israel war on Iran, military strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats and the January operation that ousted Maduro from power.
Massie said Hegseth ordered an act of war against Venezuela without congressional authorisation. He argued that the operation went beyond arresting Maduro on drug trafficking charges and was also intended to give Washington control over Venezuela’s oil reserves.
“Secretary Hegseth executed unlawful orders effecting the removal of the President of a sovereign nation, placed boots on the ground, conducted preparatory bombardments, inflicted substantial casualties, and subsequently caused regime change, each of which constitutes acts of war,” Massie said in the impeachment resolution.
Pina believes Hegseth’s visit is partly aimed at defending Trump’s policy in Venezuela before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
“Hegseth goes to Venezuela, which is probably one of Trump’s few foreign policy successes, to show the American public that the plan they are carrying out in Venezuela benefits US national interests,” he said.
Why is Delcy Rodriguez cooperating with the US?
Rodriguez and her government welcomed the agreement, saying it will help strengthen the country’s forces and improve its training and access to technology.
Venezuelan officials have also stressed that the cooperation must respect the country’s sovereignty and constitution.
But analysts say the agreement may also signal Rodriguez’s efforts to remain in power following Maduro’s ousting.
“The simple answer is that they want to remain in power as long as possible,” Phil Gunson, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.
He said Rodriguez’s government faces considerable pressure from Washington. “If they decline to cooperate, they have been told they will suffer the same fate as Maduro, or worse.”
He also pointed to Washington’s financial leverage over Caracas.
“The US currently controls most of Venezuela’s foreign earnings, in the form of revenue from oil sales, and can cut off the funds whenever it wishes,” Gunson said.
Since Maduro’s ousting in January, revenue from Venezuelan oil sales has been deposited into US-controlled accounts, with Washington supervising the release of funds to Caracas.
According to a Department of State report released on November 12, more than $12bn from Venezuela’s oil and other natural resources passed through these accounts between January and September.
The US government said nearly 99 percent of the money had been disbursed mostly to individuals and businesses in Venezuela through commercial banks. But the agreement means Caracas depends on Washington to approve the release of money from these accounts, potentially giving the Trump administration tools to put pressure on Rodriguez’s government.
Pina described the Venezuelan government’s approach as “a calculation of survival”.
“They are capable of yielding in certain areas to the US government, as long as their hold on government is not affected or threatened,” he told Al Jazeera.
Pina also said Rodriguez was trying to buy time, particularly as Democrats prepare to take control of the US Congress in January.
“She gains time,” he said, suggesting that greater congressional scrutiny of Trump’s Venezuela policies could eventually give Caracas more room to negotiate.
What could the agreement mean for Venezuela’s military?
One of the key questions, say analysts, is whether closer cooperation with Washington could lead to changes within Venezuela’s armed forces, many of whose senior officers served under Maduro.
Gunson said much would depend on Washington’s intentions.
“Will Washington seek to reform the security forces, whose leaders it has accused of drug trafficking, human rights abuses and collaboration with Colombian guerrillas and other armed groups?” he said.
He also explained Venezuela’s military is not in a position to resist US influence.
“In its current state, the military as an institution is not in a position to resist US influence, for good or ill,” he said.
But he explained that some senior officers could try to sabotage the process if they feared prosecution or losing their positions.
Separately, Venezuelan Defence Minister Gonzalez Lopez also issued his first statement since taking office.
He said the new relationship follows the “painful events of January 3”, when US forces removed Maduro from power.
Gonzalez Lopez said military cooperation with Washington would follow Venezuela’s constitution and respect the country’s “sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity”.
He also stressed that Venezuela’s armed forces would retain control over their own leadership, command and operations.
Could the agreement lead to a greater US military presence in Venezuela?
There is no clarity on the terms of the agreement.
But Pina said the agreement seems to focus on limited military cooperation, particularly operations against armed groups and drug trafficking networks along the Venezuela-Colombia border.
Pina said the two countries could carry out joint military operations, including air raids against armed groups operating in the area.
But he believes Venezuela’s military will be reluctant to give the US a much larger role.
“The Venezuelan armed forces are not going to concede beyond that,” he said.
Pina argued that Washington needs a stronger military presence in Venezuela if it wants to maintain its influence over the country’s political transition, particularly because armed forces remain under the governing party’s control.
What does the agreement mean for Latin America?
The agreement could affect other countries, particularly neighbouring Colombia, which shares a long border with Venezuela.
Several Colombian armed groups operate on both sides of the border, including the National Liberation Army (ELN), which has been fighting the Colombian government for decades.
Pina said the joint military operations could weaken these groups and reduce their ability to operate across the border.
However, on Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella had rejected a US proposal to allow joint military operations on its territory.
But De La Espriella denied the NYT report, saying Colombia wanted to strengthen military cooperation with Washington, although the presence of foreign troops would require congressional approval.
Hegseth also rejected the report, calling it “totally false”.
Gunson said Trump sees Venezuela as a major success and as a model for US relations with Latin America. But he said the results of the midterm elections could change how governments in the region respond to Washington.
“Governments in the region that seemed bound to fall into line with the US hemispheric security policy may start to think again,” Gunson said.
Pina also believes the agreement with Venezuela could raise concerns in other Latin American countries, including Mexico, about the possibility of US military operations on their territory.
“I think what happened with Nicolas Maduro marked a before and after in Donald Trump’s regional security policy,” Pina said.
He argued that the January operation showed Washington was prepared to use military force to pursue its interests, even when such actions could violate international law.
But Pina questioned whether the agreement represents a long-term change in US policy towards the region, or is primarily a political response to the recent attempt to impeach Hegseth.

noticias.titulo: Gaza Syndrome: Why Israeli soldiers’ trauma erases Palestinian victims
noticias.resumen: Israeli soldiers describe the psychological toll of the genocide in Gaza, yet many express no remorse.
noticias.texto:
Gaza Syndrome: Why Israeli soldiers’ trauma erases Palestinian victims
In a new Al Jazeera Originals film directed by Awad Joumaa, Israeli soldiers describe the psychological toll of the genocide in Gaza, yet many express no remorse.
Editor’s note: This article contains references to suicide and graphic descriptions of combat.
If you or someone you know is at risk of suicide, support is available through international crisis helplines.
“I think our army is the most moral army in the world.”
Itay Sagi, a reservist in the Maglan unit, describes killing Hamas fighters inside Israel after October 7, 2023.
“I didn’t choose to kill people. I had to,” he says.
His grief is for his friends. Sagi wants to go back and fight. He does not mention the Palestinians killed in Gaza.
Boris Shtonda, who served with an Israeli special forces unit, lost a leg when an explosive device detonated inside a building in Gaza in November 2023, killing four of his friends.
“We lost our friends, we lost our families, we lost everything,” he says.
The Israeli soldiers in the film “Gaza Syndrome” speak of nightmares, panic, addiction and Israelis who died by suicide. They speak, too, of wanting to return to fight. In hours of testimony, the Palestinians of Gaza are almost entirely absent.
The overwhelming weight of Israel’s war has fallen on Palestinians in Gaza: their children, homes and hospitals. Israeli forces have killed at least 74,700 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, according to Al Jazeera reporting. In September 2025, an independent UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed genocide in Gaza. The soldiers in this film are part of those forces.
Guy Zaken, a military bulldozer driver, told an Israeli parliamentary committee that soldiers had to “run over “‘terrorists’, dead and alive, in the hundreds”. His co-driver, Eliran Mizrahi, spent 186 days in Gaza demolishing homes and died by suicide two days before he was due to return. “He got out of Gaza, but Gaza did not get out of him,” his mother told CNN.
The question is not whether the Israeli soldiers’ psychological injuries are real. It is what psychological injury means when it is joined to denial, impunity and the absence of remorse.
Psychological crisis
In The Wretched of the Earth, the mid-20th century psychiatrist and political philosopher Frantz Fanon observed that colonial violence inflicts severe psychiatric trauma on both the colonised and the perpetrators. When soldiers carry out systematic destruction and violence, the psychological toll cannot be separated from the political structure that enables and ignores it.
An Al Jazeera Investigative Unit examination of more than 2,500 Israeli soldiers’ social media accounts documented wanton destruction, abuse of detainees, and the use of Palestinian civilians as human shields.
The scale of the psychological crisis is growing. Nearly 30,000 Israeli soldiers and security personnel wounded since October 7 have entered the Defence Ministry’s rehabilitation system, the ministry said in October.
About 63 percent have psychological injuries, with thousands formally diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and acute stress reactions following prolonged combat exposure. The Israeli army says 22 soldiers died by suicide in 2025, one more than in 2024, up from 17 in 2023. An Israeli parliament Research and Information Center report recorded 279 suicide attempts between January 2024 and July 2025. Combat soldiers accounted for 78 percent of the deaths by suicide in 2024.
Mohanad Mustafa, a scholar of Israeli society, told Al Jazeera Israel faces “a psychological crisis among thousands of soldiers, but no moral crisis”.
He says many soldiers feel no remorse for violations of international law. “This indicates a very significant moral decline in Israeli society.”
Israel’s public culture has helped make that denial possible. Oren Ziv, an Israeli journalist with +972 Magazine, says soldiers he interviewed described “an atmosphere of revenge, that everything is allowed”. They could shoot if they saw movement, he says, or if they were bored, and “nobody will investigate it”.
Daniel Bar-Tal, a political psychologist, says soldiers in Gaza still confront Palestinian suffering “to some extent”, even when they deny it or refuse to see it.
This suppressed awareness, he said, creates a quiet, internal fracture, a psychological burden that deepens precisely because the trauma cannot be fully acknowledged or resolved without confronting the suffering of those they harmed.
Ashira Darwish, a Palestinian trauma therapist and survivor of severe trauma and torture who created Active Meditation to heal from full-body paralysis, believes Israeli soldiers can enter Gaza, shoot children and burn homes only by suppressing their own humanity. She and other trauma experts emphasise that returning reservists undergo a severe psychological transition when re-entering civilian life after engaging in continuous combat.
“Someone who can exterminate an entire people while sitting there laughing will carry a psychological impact.”
Darwish describes reservists returning from Gaza to a hospital, office or school within a week or two. She warns of anger, substance addiction, domestic conflict, and sudden outbursts of violence as untreated combat trauma manifests in everyday interactions. “Where are they supposed to go with everything they have done?”
Israel’s Observatory on Femicide recorded 34 femicides in 2025, a 48 percent rise from 23 in 2024. Firearms were the most common weapon for the first time. Women’s groups warned early in the war that combat trauma and expanded access to guns could heighten the risk of domestic violence. There is no official data proving that returning soldiers caused the rise, and the Observatory found no link between licenced guns and femicide. The warning is about a society saturated with weapons, fear and impunity, not a claim that every soldier becomes violent at home.
Impunity
In Qusra, a Palestinian village south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, the film finds the other end of that impunity. Abdul Azim al-Wadi, a former head of the village council, says Israeli settlers killed his brother Ibrahim and nephew Ahmad, shot two of his sons and burned his son’s and daughter’s homes.
“The occupation army is the continuation of the settlers’ attacks,” he says. “They play the role together.”
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.
The same impunity is visible in Gaza. In NAZA, a documentary built on anonymous testimony from Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, sources describe civilian deaths factored into military decisions and targets watched inside their homes. The Israeli army called NAZA a “manipulative depiction of reality”.
In March, Israel dropped charges against five soldiers accused of sexually abusing a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention facility.
A few do not accept the orders to serve in the army. Itamar Greenberg chose military prison over conscription. Iddo Elam said: “I do not want to hold a weapon towards innocent people.”
Their refusal matters because it shows the violence is not inevitable, and neither is the story Israel tells about it.
Bar-Tal offers his country a choice: “Cut the violence or cut the narrative.”
So far, it has chosen neither.

noticias.titulo: Charting the world’s biggest IPOs as Anthropic overtakes SpaceX
noticias.resumen: The AI company behind Claude raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering ever, at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
noticias.texto:
Charting the world’s biggest IPOs as Anthropic overtakes SpaceX
The AI company behind Claude raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering ever, at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, despite fears that AI could threaten humanity, protests over energy-hungry data centres and concerns about an AI investment bubble.
Five years ago, Anthropic raised $124m from its first investors. On Wednesday, it priced its shares at $83 each, valuing the company at roughly $1.5 trillion and making it the world’s 12th-biggest company, just behind Tesla. Its shares begin trading on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”.
Demand far outstripped expectations. Investors reportedly sought six times as many shares as were available, and Anthropic sold 980 million shares, up from the 825 million it had planned, at a price above its expected range of $70 to $78.
What is an IPO?
An initial public offering (IPO) is the process by which a private company sells shares to the public for the first time by listing on a stock exchange. The company raises money by issuing new shares, and existing owners, such as founders and early investors, can sell some of theirs.
To prepare, the company hires investment banks to value it and run the sale. The banks write a prospectus explaining its business, finances and risks.
Executives and bankers then pitch the shares to big investors to gauge demand before setting the price. Early investors are usually barred from selling for several months after the listing.
How much is Anthropic worth?
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei. It develops AI models under its Claude brand, making most of its money by selling businesses access.
Its growth has been extraordinary. In May 2026, Anthropic raised $65bn from private investors at a valuation of $965bn. Its IPO price values the company about 55 percent higher.
Anthropic confidentially filed for an IPO in June and made its registration statement public on October 26.
Its revenue reached $33.2bn in the first nine months of 2026, including $17bn in the third quarter. That represents rapid growth from the previous year, although the company continues to spend heavily on computing infrastructure.
Its November prospectus also reported a net loss of $104bn over the first nine months of the year, largely driven by non-cash accounting adjustments, and disclosed nearly $901bn in computing and infrastructure commitments.
Biggest IPOs in history
Anthropic overtook SpaceX, which raised $75bn in June by selling shares at $135 each, valuing Elon Musk’s rocket, satellite and AI company at $1.75 trillion. SpaceX’s total rose to $85.7bn after it sold extra shares following its listing.
In July, South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix raised $26.5bn when it listed on the Nasdaq, the largest US listing ever by a foreign company. It now ranks third.
Saudi Aramco, which held the record before SpaceX, is now fourth. The state-owned oil giant raised $25.6bn on Riyadh’s stock exchange in December 2019, at a valuation of about $1.7 trillion.
The rest of the top 10 are Alibaba (2014), SoftBank (2018), NTT Mobile (1998), Visa (2008), AIA (2010) and Enel (1999).

noticias.titulo: ‘Too early’ to determine impact of US blockade on Iran, with Tehran defiant
noticias.resumen: The US blockade of Iranian ports has a crippling effect on the economy, but Tehran insists its economy can survive.
noticias.texto:
‘Too early’ to determine impact of US blockade on Iran, with Tehran defiant
The US blockade of Iranian ports is having a crippling effect on the economy, but Tehran insists its economy can survive.
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s economy is expected to contract further due to the ongoing blockade of its ports by the United States, inflicting pain on tens of millions of Iranians. But experts say it is too early to tell whether Washington’s economic embargo on Tehran is having the desired outcome of either collapsing the Iranian government or forcing it to concede to US demands.
The US believes its naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and sanctions – part of its maximum pressure campaign on Tehran – are working. The US has also brought a third aircraft carrier into the region to support a potential military escalation, in what appears to be an attempt to force Tehran to capitulate further to its demands.
After a deadlock in the US-Israel war on Iran, which began with strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on February 28, Washington has demanded Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz and curb its nuclear programme.
However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure and have put forward their demands. Strikes on US interests in the region this week, including radar systems in Bahrain, have been viewed as a defiant response to the US military and economic pressure. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.
Tehran-based economist Peyman Molavi said if current conditions persist, Iran’s inflation could rise considerably over the coming months.
“This will impact parallel markets like foreign currencies, gold, the stock market and housing,” he told Al Jazeera. “But it will unfortunately have the largest impact on the commodities market, from energy to agricultural products, metals, and industrial products.”
For decades, Iran’s governments have increasingly plugged their budget deficits by printing more money, which has saddled the country with a growing money supply, feeding chronic inflation. The foreign currency crunch from disrupted oil exports due to the US military blockade has only exacerbated the situation.
Molavi estimates that the year-on-year growth of the money supply in Iran could rise to 55-60 percent from its current figure of nearly 51 percent by the end of the Persian year in late March. Paired with negative economic growth, he said annual inflation could grow to about 85 percent, and point-to-point inflation to 100 percent.
‘Count your chickens’
Iranian Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati hit back at US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran.
“Like I said, he must still count his chickens at the end of autumn before moving to winter,” he said in reference to an Iranian proverb – “It’s too early to talk about winter”.
Bessent has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027. Iran’s official figures indicated that the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar year.
Hemmati said the central bank has secured $30bn in foreign currencies to weather the pressure over the coming months, prioritising procurement of essential goods for its citizens.
“American officials believe they can achieve their goals through threats and raise something new each time; from the possibility of collapse to military threats and intensified economic pressure,” Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said on Sunday.
All overland routes to and from Iran, except for one with Iraq that was closed due to security reasons, remain open despite the US efforts to isolate Iran from its neighbours, Madanizadeh insisted.
For the seventh Iranian month of Mehr that ended on October 22, the 12-month average annual inflation was at 76.8 percent, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran. Point-to-point inflation, which compares just that month with the same month of the previous year, was at 88.7 percent.
Essential goods have already been experiencing triple-digit inflation for months, with the category of food, beverages and tobacco experiencing year-on-year inflation of 113.4 percent in October, the centre said.
Iranian social media is increasingly filled with personal stories of how most people in the country of about 90 million are rapidly losing their purchasing power.
“Everywhere you look, you could have bought the same commodity with one-fifth of the money last year,” one user wrote on X. “That’s no joke, millions of people have been crushed in between.”
Markets suffer
Saleh, a 37-year-old shopkeeper at Tehran’s Grand Bazaar who deals in electric motors for small industrial units, said both domestic and Chinese-made goods can still readily be found in the market. But supply and demand have decreased since US sanctions began to bite.
“The reason is that commodities are expensive, and there’s been a stagnation in the market and also uncertainty over what will happen next,” he told Al Jazeera, asking not to use his full name due to security reasons.
“Everyone’s looking at the dollar price, and manufacturers and clients are making their decisions based on price changes. If we sold 10 items before, now we’re selling three or four, but the price increase maintained some profit. I don’t see the market being near collapse, but there’s less business.”
Companies with an established client base are proving more resilient, he added.
Bessent hailed what is happening in Iran as “one of the fastest collapses in history”, and described the Trump-directed sanctions campaign against Iran as “the greatest economic isolation in the history of the world against a single country”.
He also compared the situation in Iran with the period preceding the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, saying the country’s economy had shrunk 22 percent over three years before the union collapsed.
Economist Molavi said the comparison may not necessarily translate into immediate economic collapse for Iran as they have fundamentally different economic models.
But he pointed out that Iran’s nominal GDP has fallen from $645bn in 2012 to about $300bn now and that it could decline further if the sanctions continue.
“With the current [level] of underinvestment, halted oil sales, disrupted exports and the sense of suspension in the economy, our economic growth will become even more negative,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Netanyahu’s last stand and the dangerous politics of survival
noticias.resumen: Facing political oblivion, Netanyahu is playing a high-stakes game that could push Israel towards violence and chaos.
noticias.texto:
Netanyahu’s last stand and the dangerous politics of survival
Facing political oblivion, Netanyahu is playing a high-stakes game that could push Israel towards violence and chaos.
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the weeks since Israel’s October 27 election to launch a series of attacks on his opponents, and has called into question the legitimacy of the vote’s result.
The longtime Israeli leader is likely on his way out of power – as long as the country’s opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, can form a viable government.
That may involve leaning on parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Netanyahu has taken the opportunity to use that to tarnish the reputations of the Arab parties, and baselessly accuse them of cheating in the elections.
The environment that Netanyahu has helped generate has led to right-wing protesters threatening civil war, and critics have also accused him of deliberately fomenting war with Iran to retain office.
Separately, the Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency, led by Netanyahu’s ally David Zini, reportedly sought permission to tap the phones of five Arab lawmakers over suspected foreign interference, and to have politicians who are Palestinian citizens of Israel arrested on election day, requests the attorney general rejected.
Opposition leaders including Yair Lapid and Joint List chief Yousef Jabareen said the measures were evidence of an “attempted coup”. Meanwhile, law enforcement officials are said to be investigating whether the prime minister’s office itself fabricated the allegations of vote-buying.
For analysts and a number of Israel’s politicians, Netanyahu’s actions reflect an overriding determination to stay in power, or, failing that, engineer a government that is reliant on the support of him and his allies.
High stakes
Netanyahu faces numerous threats to both his legacy and even his freedom that, without the kind of influence he has wielded as prime minister, could prove far-reaching.
Calls for a state inquiry into Netanyahu and his government’s failings in the run-up to the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel have persisted for almost as long as the genocidal war Israel launched on Gaza in response. Those calls have grown more urgent following a series of reports suggesting that Netanyahu had been personally warned by senior Egyptian and Emirati officials about a potential attack. Establishing a state inquiry also featured prominently on the legislative slate of the parliament’s new session last week.
Similarly, both the war in Gaza and the constitutional crisis triggered by Netanyahu’s attempts to weaken judicial oversight over the government have provided useful cover against the corruption charges he has faced since 2019. Accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases, Netanyahu has seen his trial, running since May 2020, repeatedly delayed by his duties as prime minister. If found guilty, Netanyahu could face a prison sentence of up to a decade.
“Netanyahu is behaving like a wounded animal,” said Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman, of King’s College London. “For him, losing the elections is not just a political but also a personal matter, not least because of his corruption trial, which could result in him being sent to jail. Losing the premiership is losing his shield. Hence, for Netanyahu, nothing is off the table.”
Risk of violence
The chance of political violence in Israel has increased. In the days after the election, right-wing protesters gathered outside Eisenkot’s home, warning him not to form a government with the Arab-led parties, and calling him a “traitor”.
And in a letter shared publicly, Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod, a former head of Haifa’s rabbinical court, evoked the religious edict of din rodef, the “law of the pursuer”, the same principle invoked by Yigal Amir to justify his killing of former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995 over the Oslo Accords agreement with the Palestinians.
“The longer it takes for Eisenkot to form a government, the higher the risk of political violence becomes,” said Ofer Cassif, a member of parliament representing the left-wing Hadash party. “Netanyahu is willing to do anything, and I mean anything, to stay in power. He’s a psychopath. People on the right talk about civil war, and I’m not ready to discount that … Netanyahu built a cult around him, and it may easily raise arms against his rivals.”
It remains unclear what, if any, immediate legal consequences Netanyahu may face for his alleged efforts to undermine the legitimacy of the election.
Aides accused of passing false information to the police on the eve of the election could face criminal scrutiny, while Shin Bet chief Zini could see both his agency’s independence and his own position fundamentally undermined by allegedly participating in efforts to subvert the democratic process.
“Netanyahu battles for his survival and doesn’t care if those around him disappear into oblivion, but he might not succeed this time,” said Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House. “He doesn’t care about them, or even his political legacy. All he cares about is survival, about fighting for the next day and trying to cling on, no matter what the cost.”

noticias.titulo: Could Trump, Putin and Xi end the nuclear age?
noticias.resumen: Their meeting could revive the dream of nuclear disarmament that Reagan and Gorbachev nearly realised 40 years ago.
noticias.texto:
Could Trump, Putin and Xi end the nuclear age?
Their meeting in China could revive the dream of nuclear disarmament that Reagan and Gorbachev nearly realised 40 years ago.
Excitement abounds around the possible tripartite meeting in Shenzhen, China, between Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump during the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Some are calling it Yalta 2.0. We’d rather think of it as Reykjavik 2.0, while also welcoming some of the broader diplomatic breakthroughs and global reordering achieved at Yalta almost 82 years ago.
Dmitri Trenin, who directed the Carnegie Moscow Center for many years and is now president of the Russian International Affairs Council, wrote encouragingly: “The US president has mentioned that an unprecedented trilateral meeting… would make sense if it were focused on denuclearisation.” Trenin wrote this in Al Jazeera while explaining why Russia could play a helpful role in negotiating a new nuclear agreement between its Iranian ally and the United States.
While anything that might help end the dangerous, destructive, and potentially apocalyptic conflagration in Southwest Asia would be more than welcome, we think the leaders can and should aim even higher: Why not rekindle the spirit of the 1986 meeting between US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, at which they came within a hair’s breadth, arguably one word, of agreeing to eliminate not only all ballistic missiles, as Reagan originally proposed, but all nuclear weapons, as Gorbachev countered. Reagan replied, “Yes, all”, and Secretary of State George Shultz agreed. “Let’s do it,” he said.
The chance to achieve the most extraordinary diplomatic breakthrough in history slipped through Reagan’s grasp when he insisted on unlimited testing of his Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) fantasy rather than limiting SDI to the laboratory for 10 years. The world’s hopes were dashed, and we have not come close since.
Sure, we’re up against obstacles, and the odds are long. Trump has responded to the midterm shellacking by appointing Stephen Miller as chief of staff, in effect giving the middle finger to those who didn’t support the Republicans, which is not a hopeful sign. Putin knows that much of Russia’s power comes not from its economic prowess or its conventional military but from possessing the largest nuclear arsenal in the world. And Xi has made it clear that China won’t engage in arms control talks until the largest nuclear arsenals are reduced – meanwhile, China has been rapidly increasing the size of its arsenal.
That said, there are good reasons why all three could support this proposal. After his party’s midterm defeat, Trump, probably the most recalcitrant of the three, may be desperate for an achievement that could cement at least a piece of a positive legacy – and in this case a very big piece, a resounding piece. And he has been all over the map on the nuclear issue. In February 2025, he said, “There’s no reason for us to be building brand-new nuclear weapons. We already have so many. You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.” He also said, “We’re all spending a lot of money that we could be spending on other things that are actually, hopefully, much more productive.”
This is apparently something he’s been contemplating for many years. In 2016, he told Maggie Haberman and David Sanger of The New York Times: “I personally think it’s the biggest problem the world has, nuclear capability. I think it’s the single biggest problem… Power of weaponry today is beyond anything ever thought of, or even, you know, it’s unthinkable, the power… And to me, it’s the single biggest, it’s the single biggest problem.” He credits his “very brilliant” MIT physicist uncle, John Trump, with making him aware of this danger.
In 1986, he sought the advice of Bernard Lown, cofounder of International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW), which won the Nobel Peace Prize, on negotiating nuclear disarmament with Gorbachev. He told Lown he would get Reagan to send him to Moscow and that he would secure disarmament and end the Cold War in one hour. Lown commented, “I sat there dumbfounded. ‘Who is this self-inflated individual? Is he sane or what?’”
On January 23, 2025, Trump told the World Economic Forum in Davos: “And I will tell you that President Putin really liked the idea of – of cutting way back on nuclear. And I think the rest of the world, we would have gotten them to follow. And China would have come along too. China also liked it. Tremendous amounts of money are being spent on nuclear, and the destructive capability is something that we don’t even want to talk about today, because you don’t want to hear it. It’s too depressing. So, we want to see if we can denuclearise, and I think that’s very possible. And I can tell you that President Putin wanted to do it. He and I wanted to do it. We had a good conversation with China. They would have been involved, and that would have been an unbelievable thing for the planet.”
Whether Trump is sane is even more heatedly debated today than it was 40 years ago, but the possibility that he is iconoclastic enough to take a dramatic step that reverses the course of history should not be in doubt. The question is whether he’s capable of taking such a step in favour of humanity rather than against it.
The same is true of Putin. Putin told a meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club in Sochi in 2017, “Should you ask me if nuclear disarmament is possible, I will tell you: Yes, it is possible. Does Russia wish to achieve universal nuclear disarmament or not? The answer is in the affirmative, too. Yes, it does, and it will be working for it.”
Shortly before the invasion of Ukraine, the leaders of the US, Russia, China, France, and the United Kingdom jointly declared: “We affirm that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought… We remain committed to our Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) obligations, including our Article VI obligation to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament.”
Sceptics will rightly point out that this was before the invasion of Ukraine and a series of slightly veiled nuclear threats that Putin issued. But it at least offers a glimmer of hope, especially in the context of a security agreement that promises peaceful coexistence for all participants.
In 2017, in a speech at the United Nations Office in Geneva, Xi said clearly, “Nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humankind, should be completely prohibited and ultimately destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons.”
While not disavowing this sentiment, Xi has more recently indicated that China would not participate in arms control discussions until the gap between its arsenal and those of the largest nuclear powers – the United States and Russia – had narrowed. Fine. To most people, that means China increasing the size of its arsenal to the 5,000-plus weapons that both Russia and the United States possess.
We have a different proposal: How about if the US and Russia reduce their arsenals to the 600 or so that China now possesses?
We see this being done in three four-year stages, much as Reagan and Gorbachev envisioned 40 years ago. In the first stage, the US and Russia pare down their arsenals, while China forgoes its expansion. During this trust-building stage, the wars in Iran and Ukraine would need to end quickly, alongside a recommitment to the UN Charter and peaceful development by not just China, Russia, and the US, but all nuclear-armed states.
The second four-year stage would be more complex, as it would involve bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral negotiations among all nine nuclear-armed states to address the specific reasons why each of the states possesses nuclear weapons and find ways to reduce or eliminate those incentives. Intense diplomacy would be required during this period, resulting in all nine nuclear powers joining the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW). The TPNW would give all nine states a 10-year timeline to eliminate their arsenals.
However, they could accomplish this in four years, given that the starting point would be arsenals of no more than 600 nuclear warheads. This last four-year stage would involve reductions, verification, and eventual elimination of arsenals. It could be done in plenty of time for the centennial celebration of the United Nations and the centennial commemoration of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
The nuclear age should end well before it turns 100.
If Reagan and Gorbachev could come so close 40 years ago, we should not rule out the possibility that Putin, Xi, and Trump could do so today. As John Kennedy said in his great American University commencement address in 1963: “Our problems are man-made – therefore, they can be solved by man. And man can be as big as he wants. No problem of human destiny is beyond human beings. Man’s reason and spirit have often solved the seemingly unsolvable – and we believe they can do it again.”
A version of this article first appeared on Al Jazeera Arabic.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Grand Theft Auto VI launches to rave reviews after 13-year wait
noticias.resumen: Critics hail GTA 6 as a 'masterpiece', 'spectacular', and an 'astonishing American epic'.
noticias.texto:
Grand Theft Auto VI launches to rave reviews after 13-year wait
Critics hail GTA 6 as a ‘masterpiece’, ‘spectacular’, and an ‘astonishing American epic’.
Grand Theft Auto VI has launched to rave reviews, in one of the most hotly anticipated releases in gaming history.
Gamers got their hands on the latest instalment of the GTA franchise on Thursday, as critics hailed the open-world game as a “masterpiece”, “spectacular”, and an “astonishing American epic”.
The immersive game had an aggregate score of 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, based on more than 150 reviews, as it began dropping on game consoles worldwide from midnight.
“Exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played,” critic Luke Reilly wrote in a gushing review for gaming website IGN.
“Accepting that GTA 6 is very much not real also makes it all the more astonishing how much the game is very real,” reviewer Jordan Minor wrote in PCMag.
Grand Theft Auto VI follows the exploits of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a Bonnie and Clyde-like duo who become entangled in a criminal conspiracy after a seemingly easy score goes awry.
Players have free rein to explore the hyper-realistic fictional state of Leonida and its coastal metropolis of Vice City, stand-ins for Florida and Miami.
Like previous entries in the series, Grand Theft Auto VI features graphic depictions of crime and violence, with players able to mow down pedestrians in stolen vehicles and engage in shootouts with police.
The game, developed by New York-based Rockstar Games at an estimated cost of more than $1bn, is the first instalment in the series since the release of Grand Theft Auto V in 2013.
Originally set to go on sale in 2025, the release was delayed twice to allow developers to polish up gameplay.
Grand Theft Auto VI, which is available on the PlayStation 5 and the Xbox Series, is likely to be the most lucrative release in the history of the gaming industry, which is projected to be worth as much as $350bn by the end of the decade.
Pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto VI exceeded an estimated 15.8 million units as of November 17, generating $1.54bn in revenue, according to the market intelligence platform Sensor Tower.
The GTA series began in 1997 with the launch of Grand Theft Auto, a 2D top-down open-world game available on the personal computer, PlayStation and Game Boy Color.

noticias.titulo: The Xi-Putin-Trump summit will not be a ‘new Yalta’
noticias.resumen: The three leaders have divergent geopolitical goals and visions for the world order.
noticias.texto:
The Xi-Putin-Trump summit will not be a ‘new Yalta’
The three leaders have divergent geopolitical goals and visions for the world order.
On November 19, the leaders of China, the United States and Russia will gather for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on the sidelines of an annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The three have never met for formal trilateral talks, and some commentators are already calling the meeting “historic”.
In Moscow, many observers see the gathering as a “new Yalta” – another conference to divide the world into spheres of influence, similar to the one held in 1945 between Britain, the USSR and the US.
This thinking reflects Russian President Vladimir Putin’s own worldview. It is perhaps unsurprising that he was the one to propose the trilateral meeting during a call with US President Donald Trump in October.
A “new Yalta”, however, appears to be more of a case of wishful thinking than a realistic possibility. In 1945, the Soviet Union, the US and Britain came together after emerging victorious from the second world war, in which they fought against a common enemy. Today, not only do they find themselves on opposing sides of various conflicts and disputes, but they also seem to disagree on how the world should run.
While all three powers speak of a new, multipolar world and formally reject the language of hegemony, they seem to have divergent understandings of what that means.
Moscow, for example, seeks to establish itself as one of the poles in a multipolar world and a regional leader in Eurasia.
Washington, on the other hand, wants to secure its status as the pre-eminent power, while Beijing remains preoccupied with pulling the Global South away from US leadership.
Therefore, the US and China are championing a bipolar system – a world shaped by the “G2” as Trump calls it – which Russia might be unhappy with but has no means of stopping.
This disparity of aspirations is also apparent at the economic level. While Russia has chosen a path towards archaisation and opposes almost any manifestations of progress, the US and China are leading the world in technological innovation and competing in spheres such as semiconductor production, mobile communications, space exploration, robotics, biotechnology and, most recently, artificial intelligence (AI). In all these spheres, Russia has fallen behind not years, but decades.
These divergent visions are reflected in the apparent disagreement over what this summit should be about.
Trump has said he would prefer to address nuclear disarmament, a topic that is unpopular in China given that it has the smallest nuclear arsenal of the three countries. Russia, too, is not very eager given that it is relying on its nuclear arsenal as the last remaining element of its great-power status.
Putin, on the other hand, wanted to focus the summit on the settlement of the Ukraine war without the Ukrainians and Europeans present. Yet, it is unclear what can be achieved in a sit-down with Trump and Xi Jinping, given Putin’s maximalist demands.
As the recent consultations in Abu Dhabi and Moscow demonstrated, the Russian president wants profound changes to the current European order that simply cannot be secured because they would be in violation of international law.
Even if a rollback of NATO might appeal to China, Putin’s insistence on violating the principle of sovereignty would be too much for Beijing. Therefore, I cannot imagine President Xi willingly engaging in discussions that are bound to face a dead end.
Instead of entertaining his guests’ unrealistic agendas, Xi is likely to yield to no more than a general declaration on cooperation and common understanding.
For him, the summit is a long-awaited – and much-deserved – foreign policy triumph, and an acknowledgement of China’s standing in the world.
After all, he will be hosting the leaders of the two states that Beijing had looked up to as superpowers for the better part of the last century. From the late 1940s, China was highly dependent on the USSR, and even after the Mao-Khrushchev break, it replicated many Soviet policies and technologies.
Then with the launch of market reforms in the late 1970s, Beijing gradually became the most talented disciple of the US-led West, masterfully convincing the Americans that its economic rise would benefit everyone while capturing global markets through formal acknowledgement of World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and intellectual property laws.
In this sense, it is highly symbolic that China welcomes the leaders of Russia and the US at a time when it dominates global manufacturing and trade, has the fastest-growing economy of the three powers, and is a frontrunner in the global technology race.
There is also quite the contrast between the level-headed Xi and his US and Russian counterparts, whose irresponsible policies have dragged their countries into disastrous wars they cannot win or get out of.
In the end, the summit may lay the foundations of a new trilateral format between China, the US and Russia. Each leader may have their own reasons to maintain it: Trump would like to continue with his unilateral policies, sidelining traditional allies; Putin desperately wants to become a part of something reminiscent of the old times when Moscow was a superpower; and Xi might use this format to institutionalise a G2+1, knowing that the +1 – Russia – will be dropped after the Ukraine war ends and the world’s attention to the Kremlin diminishes.
Yet, little of substance would come out of these meetings. These would not be venues where the pressing issues of the world would be resolved.
And in any case, Xi, Trump and Putin may not be capable of resolving them. After all, they belong to an outgoing generation of policymakers representing a world captured not so much by powerful ideologies or leadership aspirations, but rather by memories, nostalgia, old phobias and prejudices.
In the coming years, it may happen – as it did after the “old Yalta” – that they no longer occupy positions of power and a new generation will take their place, leading the world into a better future.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Ecuadorian footballer gets eight-year ban for throwing rock at referee
noticias.resumen: Jhon Perlaza threw a stone that struck an assistant referee, who later required surgery, during a third-tier match.
noticias.texto:
Ecuadorian footballer gets eight-year ban for throwing rock at referee
Jhon Perlaza threw a stone that struck an assistant referee, who later required surgery, during a third-tier match.
Football authorities in Ecuador have handed an eight-year ban to player Jhon Perlaza after he threw a stone that struck an assistant referee during a third-tier match last month.
“The assistant referee suffered serious injuries that required surgery and a 60-day recovery period,” Ecuador’s football federation (FEF) said in a statement announcing the sanction on Wednesday.
The incident occurred during the 96th minute of the match between Perlaza’s side Club Ciudad de Yantzaza and Club Rio Aguarico FC on October 17. The match was abandoned after assistant referee Lenin Giovanni Ojeda Nunez was struck.
“The disciplinary committee found the player responsible for physical aggression against a match official and suspended him for eight years from all football-related activity, until October 19, 2034.
“In addition, the FEF will ask FIFA to extend this sanction worldwide.”
The FEF added that Yantzaza would have to pay a fine of $2,000 as well as a further $4,369.73 to cover the assistant referee’s medical expenses.
In a statement released on October 20, Yantzaza apologised to the refereeing team and fans for the incident.
“As an institution, we categorically reject all acts of aggression, whether verbal or physical, both inside and outside sporting venues. We firmly believe that football should be a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play,” they said.
“Once the person responsible for this regrettable incident was identified, the institution made the decision to remove him immediately, and he is therefore no longer part of our club.”

noticias.titulo: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What’s at stake?
noticias.resumen: World court to issue key verdict in its first genocide ruling in more than a decade.
noticias.texto:
ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What’s at stake?
World court to issue key verdict in its first genocide ruling in more than a decade.
The top court of the United Nations is scheduled to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in a case brought by the West African nation of The Gambia.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is to deliver its verdict on Thursday in what will be its first judgement on the merits of a genocide case in more than a decade.
Legal experts said the ruling could bear on South Africa’s ongoing case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, which Israel is contesting.
The Gambia accuses Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people during a 2017 military crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands to flee. Myanmar, meanwhile, claims it was responding to attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) on police posts.
Here’s what we know:
What happened to the Rohingya in Myanmar?
Myanmar’s military began what it called clearance operations in Rakhine State in October 2016 and a far larger campaign in August 2017 after attacks on police posts by a Rohingya armed group. About 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 740,000 forced to flee to Bangladesh, the UN estimated.
UN investigators found that soldiers razed hundreds of villages, carried out mass killings and routinely raped and gang-raped Rohingya women, girls and boys. They said the sexual violence indicated genocidal intent.
The military itself has announced convictions in only two cases brought after the violence. However, in one, seven soldiers jailed for killing 10 Rohingya men and boys at Inn Din village were freed after serving less than a year of their 10-year sentences.
In 1982, long before the crackdown, Myanmar excluded the Rohingya from its 135 recognised ethnic groups, calling them immigrant Bengalis despite many families having lived in Myanmar for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since then, making them the world’s largest stateless group.
Since fighting with the military resumed in 2023, the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has taken most of the state. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights said in August that both forces have committed widespread and systematic abuses against the Rohingya, accusing the Arakan Army of torture, sexual violence and forced recruitment.
The UN said those abuses have driven more than 155,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh since early 2024, taking the refugee population there up to about 1.2 million.
Nearly all the refugees live in crowded camps in the Cox’s Bazar District, where they are dependent on international aid that has fallen sharply in recent years, particularly since United States President Donald Trump’s administration slashed foreign aid in 2025. Most refugees now receive smaller food rations, and many camp schools have closed. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned that recent arrivals often lack sufficient food, clean water and healthcare.
Why did The Gambia take Myanmar to the ICJ?
The Gambia said it brought the case after decades of persecution of the Rohingya that culminated in the 2017 operation, which it argued breached the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The Muslim-majority nation of 2.5 million people filed the case in November 2019 on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The case was led by Abubacarr Tambadou, then The Gambia’s attorney general and justice minister.
In January 2020, the court ordered Myanmar to take emergency measures to prevent genocidal acts.
Myanmar initially argued that The Gambia, which was not directly involved in the conflict, could not bring the case. But in 2022, judges ruled that it could because both countries are parties to the convention, under which all signatories are obligated to prevent and punish genocide.
Hearings on the merits of the case followed in January this year with seven states – including Canada, France and the United Kingdom – backing The Gambia.
What exactly is the ICJ being asked to decide?
The judges must decide whether Myanmar, as a state, committed genocide against the Rohingya, thereby breaching the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
The ICJ passes judgements on state actions. It does not rule on the criminal guilt of individual soldiers or commanders.
Under the convention, “genocide” refers to acts such as killing and causing serious harm committed with intent to destroy, wholly or partly, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
Evidence that a state has committed atrocities is not enough. The court must also find they were carried out with specific intent to destroy a group. Such intent can be shown through direct statements or orders or inferred from a pattern of conduct.
The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference from Myanmar’s conduct.
Myanmar, meanwhile, said it was conducting a legitimate counterterrorism operation against Rohingya fighters, not targeting Rohingya people as a whole.
What would a genocide finding mean for the Rohingya?
A genocide finding would formally recognise the harm the Rohingya have suffered but may do little in the short term for the more than one million victims of violence and displacement, said Michael Becker, an international law professor at Trinity College Dublin and a former ICJ legal officer.
The Gambia wants the court to order Myanmar to ensure displaced Rohingya can return safely to their land, compensate them, and replace or rebuild destroyed homes and property.
Becker told Al Jazeera the court may impose those demands only partly or in general terms, leaving Myanmar to decide how to comply with them.
Such an outcome would “surely be disappointing” to those who are sceptical that the government would fulfil those demands in good faith, he said.
“Even if the ICJ were to order far-reaching forms of relief, the political conditions on the ground in Myanmar are not amenable to realising that relief anytime soon,” Becker said.
He said a finding would instead have to be used to pressure Myanmar diplomatically.
William Schabas, an international law professor at Middlesex University in the UK, said the measures that The Gambia was seeking on behalf of the Rohingya were “robust” even though they fell short of demanding citizenship, which would end their statelessness.
“Assuming Myanmar implements the conclusions, this will indeed have significant positive effects on the security, dignity and livelihoods of the Rohingya in Myanmar,” Schabas told Al Jazeera.
What could the ruling mean for future genocide cases?
The Myanmar ruling will be the first final judgement out of five genocide cases pending before the ICJ.
Becker said the outcome could clarify the court’s longstanding “only reasonable inference” test. Under it, judges infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct only if no other reasonable explanation fits.
He said the court’s two rulings on the Balkan wars left it unclear whether genocide could be deemed to occur alongside armed conflict, which he said was “an unduly restrictive standard”.
Thursday’s judgement could instead treat armed conflict as an alternative explanation for a party’s conduct, rather than an automatic bar to establishing genocidal intent, he said.
According to Schabas, the ruling will “have very dramatic effects” on the outcome of the other pending cases, particularly the case against Israel.
“In my opinion, the South African case against Israel is much stronger than the case of Gambia against Myanmar. If Gambia wins against Myanmar, we can be confident that South Africa will prevail over Israel,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Far from Trump-Putin meeting, Europe to count cost of Ukraine’s defence
noticias.resumen: European leaders set to meet in Berlin as Kyiv faces a 25 billion-euro ($27.4bn) financing gap next year.
noticias.texto:
Far from Trump-Putin meeting, Europe to count cost of Ukraine’s defence
European leaders set to meet in Berlin as Kyiv faces a 25 billion-euro ($27.4bn) financing gap next year.
As US President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China, European leaders are due to gather in Berlin to agree on funding for Ukraine’s defence and press Washington’s visiting envoys for a European role in Russia-Ukraine peace talks.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting the so-called Coalition of the Willing summit on Thursday alongside French President Emmanuel Macron and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. More than 30 leaders are expected to attend, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The summit agenda includes long-term security guarantees and continued military and financial support for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has said air defence will be his immediate priority as Kyiv enters a winter with the threat of Moscow’s drone attacks looming.
Trump administration envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected, according to media reports, to meet Ukrainian officials and Europe’s newly formed negotiating team in Berlin. The team includes France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, plus European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
Washington has backed European participation in the next round of talks, but Moscow has yet to agree.
The impasse could put Ukraine’s main financial backer on the sidelines of talks over its future, as European Union countries are set to make even steeper commitments.
The European Commission on Wednesday proposed an additional 45 billion-euro ($49.3bn) loan for 2027, with up to 25 billion euros ($27.4bn) for military aid and 20 billion euros ($21.9bn) for budget support. That follows a 1.71 billion-euro ($1.87bn) payment on Monday under an existing EU loan for drones, ammunition and air defence.
Even if the new loan is approved, it would leave a 25 billion-euro ($27.4bn) financing gap next year.
‘Quite a stupid thing’
Zelenskyy said the US envoys had promised to brief Kyiv on Trump’s discussions in China, where he is meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin.
The Berlin summit gives European negotiators a chance to agree on what they want from the next round and put it directly to Trump’s envoys, just days after a public disagreement between the transatlantic partners emerged in Brussels.
At Tuesday’s Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting at NATO headquarters, Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for policy, argued that some Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia had done little to slow Moscow’s military advances and that attacks on civilian infrastructure may have hardened Russian resolve.
In a swift backlash, German Federal Minister of Defence Boris Pistorius called the assessment “quite a stupid thing” and pointed to Russia’s repeated attacks on Ukraine’s electricity and heating infrastructure. London was quick to align with Berlin, with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting arguing that Ukraine should decide how to fight and that its long-range strikes had weakened Russia’s military capabilities.
After a nine-month hiatus, US, Ukrainian and Russian officials resumed talks in Abu Dhabi last week. Witkoff and Kushner then met Putin in Moscow and said Europeans would join the next round, despite Moscow throwing cold water on the idea.
Europe gets a seat at the table
Within Europe, newfound energy has emerged with the prospect of the bloc joining negotiations, with EU leaders agreeing in Dublin last week on a team.
Sharon Hudson-Dean, a senior fellow with the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera that “success” in Berlin would mean firmer commitments to Ukraine’s immediate defence and its 2027 budget, as well as closer alignment between Washington and European capitals.
European leaders, she said, are wary of US announcements and Russian intentions and want a say in decisions that will affect their security, budgets and markets.
“Washington should leave Berlin recognising that Europe will shoulder much of the financial and security burden of implementing any settlement, and as such, needs a seat at the table,” Hudson-Dean said.
With Europeans likely to bear many of the costs of security guarantees, sanctions and Ukraine’s path to EU membership, she said, they want to be “in on the takeoffs, not just the crash landings”.
Ahead of the Berlin summit, European allies pledged more winter aid for Kyiv and outlined plans to deliver fighter jets and air defence missiles, as Zelenskyy urged them to release Patriot and IRIS-T interceptors from their stocks, offering to replace them with missiles Kyiv has on order.
The Ukrainian leader also said Ukraine needed 40 more F-16s.
In response, Germany and Norway each announced $300m for the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a NATO-coordinated programme that buys US weapons for Ukraine. Their joint package includes Patriot missiles.
The UK, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland, Belgium, France, Sweden, Lithuania, Estonia and Portugal all reiterated or pledged further funding for Ukraine in the lead-up to the Berlin summit.
European rifts
Poland will be represented on Europe’s negotiating team, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday that Warsaw would put no additional money into PURL at this stage. Bulgaria, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia have indicated they will opt out of the next round of EU financing.
Despite elections in Hungary that ushered in a more EU-friendly leadership, Budapest continues to oppose military assistance for Kyiv.
Kinga Koranyi, an assistant professor at the University of Wroclaw who studies Hungarian politics and EU governance, told Al Jazeera the idea that Hungary should “stay out of the war” remains widely shared after years of politicisation under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s Fidesz party, leaving direct funding for Kyiv unpopular.
Years of lost access to EU funds over rule-of-law disputes have also made Budapest cautious about new spending, she said, as the cost of the war with no end in sight continues to mount.
