noticias.texto:
A new online safety act is likely to be needed to tackle convicted criminals such as Russell Brand using social media platforms to broadcast messages from prison, Labour MP Jess Phillips has said.
Just days after his conviction, Brand’s wife, Laura, broadcast a message from her husband to their 6.6 million YouTube subscribers, claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences for which he had been convicted by a jury. The video has had almost 850,000 views.
The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) launched an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules. Google, which owns YouTube, has rejected a UK government request, made via the Prison Service, for the video to be taken down amid warnings that it was causing distress to sexual abuse survivors.
A Google spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.”
Phillips, a former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, admitted the government did not have the power to compel platforms to remove distressing content of this kind.
“Ofcom codes on women’s safety online are just voluntary and frankly voluntary codes to tech companies is the triumph of hope over experience,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
“This is an entirely new era and frankly the regulations are almost certainly not in place for the government to just demand that this be taken down.”
Passed in 2023, the Online Safety Act works to protect social media users from illegal content, as well as ensuring under-18s are not exposed to content that is not age-appropriate, such as pornography. It is being introduced on a phased basis and was expanded this year by additional legislation, updating Ofcom codes of practice. It does not explicitly address the issue of prisoners using social media platforms to directly communicate with the outside world, which in light of Brand’s platform, Phillips accepts is not sufficient.
“Regulatory frameworks, changes and potentially a second online safety act is needed, because before we haven’t had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings,” she said.
Phillips said that pressure would continue to build on organisations such as Google.
“All Google do by leaving this up is show that those codes are not good enough,” she added.
“I think it [a new online safety act] is very likely and the more that these companies show that they are not putting victims at the absolute heart of their policymaking in their content within their own content schemes. If Google want less regulation they will take this down.”
Calls by voices including the victims’ commissioner for London, Andrea Simon, for action to be taken by Google were joined on Thursday morning by ministers.
“I hope they make the same decision that Meta has,” said the minister for children and families, Josh MacAlister, noting that the parent company of Facebook had disabled Brand’s social media accounts on the basis they breached standards prohibiting accounts that were “harmful to the community”.
Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, told Sky News: “It’s quite a disturbing video, actually, but abhorrent in the message it’s conveying.”
“Imagine if you’re one of the victims of Brand’s heinous crimes and you see that video. Prisoners are already banned from making statements to the media. We think this is an exceptional case where MoJ ministers have asked Google to remove this specific content and we hope they’ll do so.”
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said she was concerned if prisoners were able to use conduits in prison to send messages, but felt that Brand’s wife was a separate person and YouTube was “a private platform”.
“Immediately demanding that private platforms take down without looking at whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from,” she said.
While the Brand case has brought the issue into sharp focus, there has been concern in the past about the continued ability to retain a presence on social media of other figures such as Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson.

noticias.titulo: EDF snaps up 1.3m more customers after Utilita takeover
noticias.resumen: Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier brings account base up to 6m after purchase of pay-as-you-go supplier EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita. Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita.
Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed.
The pair will continue to serve their customers independently until the deal concludes. Utilita customers will be contacted about any changes to their service.
After the deal, EDF has promised to continue to operate from Utilita’s headquarters near Southampton which is the base for about 600of Utilita’s employees.
EDF, which is owned by the French state, set out the takeover plans a year after it completed a deal to take on 47,000 standard credit accounts from Utilita which said it hoped to sharpen its focus on smart pay-as-you-go customers.
The deal is likely to have helped bolster Utilita’s financial position, which briefly fell short of the industry regulator Ofgem’s tougher new financial resilience tests in an industry assessment in September 2025.
Utilita confirmed that it was one of five suppliers which had failed to meet Ofgem’s financial rules last year, but said it was able to comply with the standards within months of the regulator’s red flag.
For EDF, the deal will help to bolster its business as most large suppliers continue to lose customers to smaller rivals. EDF lost about 280,000 customer accounts in the year after July 2025, while British Gas, Scottish Power and E.ON Next were also losing customers. Octopus Energy, the country’s largest supplier, is the only big energy company which has continued to grow its market share.
Utilita was founded in 2003 as a specialist prepay energy supplier, and became the first supplier to install a smart meter in 2008.
Its pioneering approach to smart metering helped the company to modernise pay-as-you-go energy by allowing customers to top-up via an app, website, or by phone rather than visit a corner shop or post office to pay for credit on a plastic card or key.
Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF’s UK business, said Utilita would bring “further expertise” to the supplier, marking “a significant step” in EDF’s ambition to grow its UK customer business.
“Together, we will have the scale and skills to keep developing services and support for the households who rely on us,” Rossi said.
Bill Bullen, the founder of Utilita, said the deal would ensure that Utilita could continue to provide “best-in-class smart prepay solutions to Britain’s households”.
Last month, German energy group E.ON Next completed a deal to buy struggling UK rival Ovo after the deal was approved by Britain’s competition watchdog.
The deal comes as households prepare for a sharp rise in energy bills this winter. On Wednesday, the consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast the quarterly industry price cap would jump 26% from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.

noticias.titulo: BAE to slash 1,000 jobs across head office and air business to streamline orders
noticias.resumen: Job cuts to exclude shop floor, aircraft maintenance and trainees but move prompts calls for more orders to support British defence giant BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, triggering calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor. The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, triggering calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor.
The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”.
The cuts represent about 2% of its 50,000 strong workforce in the UK, which includes about 18,500 in its air business and about 1,000 in its head office in London. They will be made through voluntary redundancies and will exclude people working on the shop floor, aircraft maintenance at RAF bases and early career trainees.
A spokesperson for BAE said the cuts represented the “next stage of our ongoing focus on enhancing our agility and competitiveness, so we can help to maximise the value of every pound our customers spend on defence.
“We recognise that this news may be unsettling for our people and we’re focused on achieving potential workforce reductions through a voluntary process,” they said.
BAE last year received an order for 20 Typhoon fighter jets from Turkey, in a deal announced at the factory by Keir Starmer. However, that order is thought to provide only two years of work at the Lancashire factories – not enough to sustain jobs until production starts on the next generation of fighters. BAE will lead production of the sixth-generation Tempest fighter in an alliance with Italy and Japan.
A source with knowledge of the matter said that the job cuts were linked to uncertainty over the Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet programme, more than cost-cutting.
The move comes even as BAE has benefited from a boom in defence spending since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, the company told its investors it had secured £33bn in orders so far this year and that it expected further contracts before the end of 2026. It also raised its free cashflow guidance for its financial year by 10%, from about £2bn to £3bn.
Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the union Unite, warned that there would not be a manufacturing industry left in the UK “if the government doesn’t start making critical decisions”.
“To stop the erosion of defence jobs and get the growth we need, the government needs to announce contracts for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) immediately,” she said.
BAE unveiled the uncrewed CCA – which is named Brontanax – at the Farnborough International airshow in July.
Andrew Snowden, a Conservative MP in Lancashire where BAE has two air manufacturing hubs, echoed Graham’s call for more government support.
He told the Lancashire Post: “The government should act now to support BAE by placing orders for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft, giving skilled workers and the supply chain here in Lancashire a clear pipeline of work.”
It comes with the government also under pressure to reach a decision on its Skynet military satellite replacement. American weapons maker Lockheed Martin was thought to be the Ministry of Defence’s preferred choice, but ministers have delayed the choice after Unite argued it would lead to UK job cuts at rival Airbus’s existing factories.
An MoD spokesperson said: “We know that any potential voluntary redundancies can cause concerns and our thoughts are with those potentially affected.
“This government is delivering the biggest boost in defence spending since the cold ar, having already agreed £4bn worth of investments since July.
“This includes awarding BAE a £708m contract extension to lead the Global Combat Air Programme developments and supporting the £8bn contract to supply Turkey with 20 Typhoon jets last year, which sustains 6,000 jobs at two BAE sites.”

noticias.titulo: Car use in London forecast to rise by 10% in next decade

noticias.texto:
Car use in London will rise by 10% over the next decade with cycling and walking falling as a proportion of trips, according to an official forecast by the city’s mayoralty, putting into doubt Sadiq Khan’s promises on air quality and the environment.
Based on projections in the draft version of the latest 10-year London plan, drawn up by the mayor’s office and Transport for London (TfL), road congestion from a growing population would slow buses down, while packed tube services might require stations to close regularly to ease numbers.
Khan’s office said the figures were not a prediction but modelling, based on an assumption of no new transport policies, and did not take into account the impact of recent changes such as the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street.
The expectation was that active travel levels would increase and car use would fall, they added.
The draft plan for 2026-36 sets out three possible models of growth in population and jobs, and thus demand for transport, housing and other services. The central one of these, seen as the most likely, forecasts a population of 9.9 million people, up from the current 9.1 million.
If this happens, according to the plan, the number of car or other motor vehicle trips would rise by 10% between a baseline date of 2023 and 2036, with trips using public transport going up by 17%.
Journeys by active travel, such as walking and cycling, would rise by 6%, resulting in a slight fall as a proportion of all trips taken.
A relative decline in active travel would put London at odds with the trajectory of many other European cities, for example Paris, where bike use almost tripled as a proportion of all trips in just five years.
Mayoral officials, however, dispute that this will actually happen, pointing to London’s recent growth in cycling and walking trips, with new cycle lanes and hundreds of school streets that restrict motor traffic at drop-off and pickup times.
An increase in car journeys would also bring what the report called “significant challenges” on the roads, including a possible 7% reduction in average speeds, slowing down bus routes.
On public transport, overcrowding would become more common, while on the underground, severe overcrowding at some stations “indicates the possible regular need for intervention during periods of peak demand, such as closing stations to entering passengers or nonstopping trains”, it warned.
The modelling calls into question Khan’s progress on greening London’s transport network, given his pledge in 2022 for a 27% reduction in car use across London by 2030.
Ralph Smyth, a strategy adviser for the Transport Action Network campaign group, who uncovered the projections in the plan, said progress on shifting the capital away from car use appeared to have stalled.
He said: “The new London Plan was the opportunity for the mayor to leave a legacy of a cleaner, healthier and less congested city. Inexplicably, he seems to want to turn back the clock and increase cars across the capital.”
Khan has made progress in cleaning up London’s air, particularly with the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone to central and inner London in 2023, but the capital lags behind some other European cities and a shift towards more driving would further stall progress, even with the adoption of electric vehicles.
The transition to EVs will help, said Jenny Bates, a campaigner from Friends of the Earth, “but this will take many years – and it won’t reduce congestion”.
“London, like many cities, needs to reduce car use and reclaim space for safer walking and cycling routes, and more urban greenery to help cool the city during increasingly hot summers,” she said.
Simon Munk, the head of campaigns for the London Cycling Campaign, said the plan risked “modelling a future that is already out of date”.
He said: “TfL should not be modelling for ongoing heavy car use in London, but instead articulating how to do land-use planning and transport policy to get a lot less of it.”
A spokesperson for the mayor said: “City hall expects active travel will increase significantly by 2036 and car use will fall.
“The modelling in the London plan is based on a scenario in which no additional active travel schemes will be introduced over the next decade – which clearly is not the case, and the modelling will help identify what future transport schemes may be needed.”

noticias.titulo: Hakeem Jeffries on brink of Senate history as he tells Democrats to ‘fight Maga, not each other’ – US politics live
noticias.resumen: Democrats resoundingly nominated Jeffries to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress is sworn in next year Denmark’s parliament on Thursday approved a hard-wrought agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. noticias.texto:
Hakeem Jeffries said it is the job of Democratic lawmakers to “fight Maga extremism” as he stood on the brink of becoming the first ever Black house speaker.
Democrats on Wednesday resoundingly nominated Jeffries to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress is sworn in next year.
A New York congressman who has served as the Democratic minority leader since 2023, Jeffries is set to become one of Donald Trump’s most prominent opponents for the final two years of his presidency, when Democrats will control both the Senate and House of Representatives and are expected to undertake aggressive efforts to check his powers.
After his nomination was secured during closed-door voting, 251-11, ahead of a full House vote, Jeffries promised to take on the Trump administration’s Maga approach to governing the US. “Our job is to fight Maga extremism, not each other,” he said, “and to get big things done for the American people.”
Democrats nominated Jeffries despite concerns from some progressives that he represents a politically risky status quo for a party that is looking to capitalize on a surprisingly good performance in the midterms, where voters swept them back into power in the House and Senate with significant majorities.
He would become the first Democratic House speaker since Nancy Pelosi, who will retire from Congress at the end of this year.
Meanwhile today, president Trump has left China after hailing his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, saying the three leaders were “really making history”. Trump said the US, Russia and China, the world’s largest nuclear powers, were “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles.
You can follow the latest from Apec in our live blog here:
In other developments:
During a fiery House hearing, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, defended his decision to take a government plane to attend a college football game, while thousands of flights had been cancelled and the airspace closed during the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) nationwide grounding over the weekend. “You want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great nieces to an [Lousiana State University] game that was scheduled for weeks prior because I wanted to be a good uncle,” Mullin said, following questions from Congressman Bennie Thompson, the homeland security committee’s top Democrat.
Elon Musk called his midterm political spending “foolish.” After pouring nearly half a billion dollars into the election, in a Wednesday conversation with The New York Times’s DealBook Summit, Musk said: “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”
US Transportation secretary Sean Duffy blamed contractor L3Harris for last week’s nationwide ground stop. As legislators press for more answers on last week’s outage that caused thousands of flights to be halted, Duffy has continued finger-pointing, telling digital media outlet 2WAY on Wednesday that L3Harris, the aerospace and defense company whose router malfunctioned during an update, did not identify the issue “quick enough.”
Trump’s contentious triumphal arch continues to face setbacks. A federal judge extended the construction ban for the arch, slated for the Memorial Circle in Washington DC. A group of veterans and members of the Kennedy family members have blasted the project as disrespectful to those interred at the Arlington national cemetery.
Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intensely with Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement since 2024.
“I’m not Maga,” the world’s richest person told the New York Times Dealbook summit, which he attended via video call from China, where he is one of several US business leaders who have accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia.
“I’m not sure what Maga means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that,” the chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla added.
Musk famously declared at a 2024 campaign rally in Madison Square Garden: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.”
In a 45-minute interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin, a New York Times columnist, Musk also said it would be good for Washington to have split control between the two parties, and that he thinks “there are positives and negatives in both”.
He also accused Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, of “lying” about restrictions on access to his firm’s Starshield satellite system; praised Jensen Huang, the ousted Nvidia chief executive; and said that “no one I met at Anthropic set off my evil detector”.
Asked about his previous negative comments about Anthropic, Musk said that before he agreed to rent computing power to the AI firm: “I went to met with a lot of people at Anthropic. I didn’t just move forward with the deal.”
“My interaction so far with the Anthropic team is that they seem like good people and they seem principled,” Musk added. “They seem diligent and they seem seem to care about the future.”
Musk donated at least $250m of his own money to help Trump win the election in 2024, and recently spent nearly $500m in the US midterms to support Republicans, many of whom lost.

The vote follows months of pressure by president Donald Trump seeking to control Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark, a Nato ally.

noticias.texto:
Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.
Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palestinian man who escaped the Nakba in 1948, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel. The story was inspired by her father, Sami Abdul-Fattah Al-Assadi, who fled the Nakba as a child with his family, before studying in Italy and moving to New York.
In a tearful speech, Assadi said, “What a beautiful story this has been, from its origins at my father’s deathbed until now, ending here and accepting this award. And so full of pain.
“In the course of its writing, I have experienced deep personal grief and unimaginable collective grief. I have watched cancer ravage my father’s body and genocide ravage his people and their children. And perhaps this is the Palestinian story on this earth. So beautiful. So painful.”
The judges praised Assadi’s “elegant lyricism” and “ambitious bending of time and space” and called the novel “a visionary, finely wrought portrait of rupture and endurance”.
Assadi won the $10,000 prize against Edwidge Danticat’s Dèy, Julián Delgado Lopera’s Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You, Valeria Luiselli’s Beginning Middle End and Morgan Thomas’ Mad Eden.
Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy won the $10,000 nonfiction prize for his debut Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, about his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt. ElGendy was unable to attend the ceremony after being denied a visa to the US, so his prize was collected by his editor Helen Thomaides, who read out his speech.
ElGendy said he had dreamed of turning his experience into a memoir as it gave him distance from the physical abuse he endured, and revealed he had practised award acceptance speeches under his duvet in prison.
“Today that dream should have come full circle but, like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camps stand ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable,” ElGendy wrote.
The New York Times speculated earlier this month that ElGendy was not even eligible for the award as he did not meet its citizenship or residency requirements after fleeing the US due to Ice deportations, but the National Book Foundation, which administers the National book Awards, disputed this and said it did not “have any concerns regarding the eligibility of his title”.
Samar Yazbek of Syria, a finalist for the books in translation category, was also denied a visa, with the National Book Foundation describing both decisions as “unjust”.
The state department declined to comment on any specific cases, but issued a statement to Associated Press saying that “the Trump Administration continues to put America and its interests first by fully enforcing US immigration laws and ensuring lawful travel through our visa process. As Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio said, ‘a visa is a privilege, not a right’.”
Publishers submitted 1,912 books to the National book awards this year, with the winners judged by panels of authors, editors, booksellers and others in the literary community.
Brenda Hillman won the $10,000 poetry category for Still House in the Desert: An eco-contemplation, praised as “a rigorously unsentimental portrait of the stillness … of the poet’s childhood home after her mother’s death”.
David Leviathan and Gabriel Duckels won the $10,000 young people’s literature category for The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America.
Indian-British author Salman Rushdie was presented with a medal for “distinguished contribution to American letters”, while paediatrician and author Perri Klass was honoured for “outstanding service to the American literary community”.
Rushdie recalled being welcomed into the US literary scene after spending years under police protection in London after the fatwa over The Satanic Verses, and used his speech to thank the late Ursula K Le Guin for liking his first novel. “She was just about the only one who did! And it meant everything to me,” he said, to laughs.
“All I want to say is that it has been quite a ride, from over there to over here,” he added. “And to ride into this town and end up in this saloon, with these companions, is a hell of a thing.”
Actor and author Kyle MacLachlan hosted the ceremony, held at Cipriani Wall Street, while singer Michelle Zauner, author of the bestselling memoir Crying in H Mart, performed onstage.

noticias.titulo: ICJ: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
noticias.resumen: The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.
noticias.texto:
ICJ: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
November 19, 2026
The International Court of Justice on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.
"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees.
What is the case about?
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predomiantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.
A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp.
The Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.
Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.
Aung San Suu Kyi, who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
What else did Judge Iwasawa say as he read out the verdict?
The ICJ said that by its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.
Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But he also said that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and if anything fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.
At one point reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.
This is a developing story, more to follow...

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Pistorius to visit Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
noticias.resumen: Germany's Defense Minister's first stop in Poland will be at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau. Follow DW for more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Pistorius to visit Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Defense Minister Oscar Pistorius talks security in Poland
- Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets
- UniCredit and Germany reach Commerzbank takeover agreement
Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from Germany on Thursday, November 19:
Defense Minister Oscar Pistorious heads to Poland
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will travel to Poland for a two-day visit.
Pistorius is scheduled to meet his Polish counterpart, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, in the capital Warsaw for talks on defense policy.
Poland is a member of both the EU and NATO and is one of the most important political and military allies of Ukraine.
The trip to Germany's neighbor to the east will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.
Auschwitz-Birkenau is one of the biggest symbols of the Holocaust and Germany's Nazi regime, with some 1.1 million people having died in the camp between 1940 and 1945, most of them Jews.
The camp's victims were shot, murdered in gas chambers or died of starvation and disease.
Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets
The German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) said in a report that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals.
According to the report, the number of hacked systems has nearly doubled within a year, with BSI reporting some 75,400 infected systems in Germany to internet providers every day, an 89% increase. Some of the gadgets were found to be already infected at the factory, the report says.
The vast majority of cases involved Android devices, particularly consumer electronics connected to the so-called "Internet of Things."
BSI said criminals rent the hijacked devices as proxy botnets on the dark web to hide their own attacks, which would allow for consumers themselves to unknowingly come under investigators' scrutiny.
BSI President Claudia Plattner has also warned of AI-driven attacks.
"The disruption coming in particular from high-performance, agentic AI has set new benchmarks," she said.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will head to Poland today to talk security with one the most important political and military allies of Ukraine.
His trip will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.
Meanwhile, Germany's Federal Office for Information Security has warned that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals
Follow this blog for more on that and other stories from Germany!

noticias.titulo: Denmark ratifies security deal with US and Greenland
noticias.resumen: The deal provides the US with expanded military access, on top of what it already had based on a previous agreement. It comes after threats by US President Trump to take Greenland with force.
noticias.texto:
Denmark ratifies security deal with US and Greenland
November 19, 2026
Denmark'sparliament on Thursday ratified a security agreement with the USover Greenland, hoping to end tensions after US President Donald Trump had repeatedly demanded control over the autonomous Danish territory.
In the Danish 179-seat parliament, all 109 members present voted in favor of the text. Greenland's parliament already ratified the deal in early November.
US ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the ratification, saying in a post on X: "The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO."
What does the Danish-US security agreement over Greenland include?
The trilateral security and military access agreement between Washington, Nuuk and Copenhagen allows for expanded US military presence on the mineral-rich and strategically located island in the northern Atlantic.
It also includes permission to establish a "Golden Dome" missile defense system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
The island is home to some 57,000 people and is strategically located along the shortest route from Europe to North America. It already is home to the northernmost US military base.
The deal was signed in September by Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen but still needed ratification from lawmakers in Greenland and Denmark.
Trump's threats to take Greenland by force
In January 2026, Trump renewed calls for Greenland to become part of the US, threatening military action and tariffs against European allies if they opposed him.
He argued that Denmark was not able to protect the autonomous Arctic territory from threats by China and Russia. His demands strained US relations with Denmark and alarmed European NATO allies.
Tensions somewhat eased in late January when Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte announced a "concept of a deal" that would expand US military access to Greenland. This then led to the agreement being signed in September.
Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has broad military access to Greenland. Denmark had repeatedly said it was open to expanding the US military presence on the island but rejected Trump's demand for full US control.

noticias.titulo: South Korea's top court overturns jail term for former PM Han
noticias.resumen: Former Prime Minister Han Duck-so was convicted of helping legitimize the 2024 martial law declaration. The case will now return to a lower court.
noticias.texto:
South Korea's top court overturns jail term for former PM Han
November 19, 2026
The South Korean Supreme Court on Thursday overturned a 15-year prison sentence for the country's former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for playing a key role in the 2024 imposition of martial law by ex-President Yoon Suk Yeol.
The case will now return to a lower court, the Seoul High Court, which had sentenced Han to 15 years in prison in May.
Why was South Korean ex-PM Han's sentence overturned?
Han was convicted for helping plan the insurrection by suggesting that Yoon hold a Cabinet meeting to make martial law seem legitimate.
He also allegedly tried to collect Cabinet members' signatures on a related document and reviewed orders to cut off power and water to media outlets critical of Yoon.
The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that prosecutors had not sufficiently proven the case and ordered a review of the conviction.
At the same time, the top court upheld a four-year prison term for Yoon's wife, Kim Keon Hee, on charges of corruption, including manipulating stock prices and bribery.
What was the 2024 insurrection?
On December 3, 2024, former president Yoon Suk Yeol abruptly declared martial law, prompting massive protests and a showdown in parliament.
At the time, Yoon said the declaration was needed to rid the country of "pro-North Korean forces" and followed it by sending troops and police into parliament.
But enough lawmakers managed to enter the assembly chamber to unanimously vote down Yoon's decree, forcing his cabinet to rescind it.
Yoon was impeached and later found guitly of leading an insurrection and sentenced to life in prison.

noticias.titulo: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
noticias.resumen: As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington.
noticias.texto:
Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
November 19, 2026
As Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support.
For Iran, relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow.
Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran. But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington.
That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate?
China is now Iran's economic lifeline
China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil.
In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports, much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions.
As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs.
Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, says China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own.
"If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW.
But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter.
"The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost said.
Sanctions enforcement raises pressure on Iran
That distinction has become more important as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports.
In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny.
As a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets.
"A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said.
Iran prepares for the worst
This economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning. A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently said the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero.
That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks.
Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating.
What does Beijing want?
Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost.
But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies.
A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping. China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability.
Russia can help, but how much?
Russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation.
Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify.
Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, believes the summit should be viewed within a larger attempt to manage the wars in both Ukraine and the Middle East.
"Russia, China and the United States appear to be seeking constructive dialogue and results that could shape a new security architecture in the international system," Vakhshiteh told DW.
Russia supports Iran, but limits remain
Solhdoost also warns against overstating Russian support for Iran.
The strategic partnership between Moscow and Tehran provides for security cooperation and efforts to counter unilateral sanctions, but it does not require Russia to enter a war on Iran's behalf.
Since Russia is deeply engaged in Ukraine, it likely has its own priorities in negotiations with Washington, says Solhdoost.
"Russia would prioritize its own national interests in negotiations with the US over Ukraine and Iran," he said.
Moscow could support Iran while simultaneously using its relationship with Tehran as leverage in talks with Trump over Ukraine.
How much influence do the three powers have?
For Iran, ties with China and Russia remain essential. They provide alternative trade routes, export markets and diplomatic support that complicate Washington's efforts to isolate Tehran.
Yet neither Beijing nor Moscow views Iran solely through the lens of strategic partnership. Both weigh support for Tehran against their own economic interests, security concerns and dealings with Washington.

noticias.titulo: India: Nearly 50,000 evacuated as Cyclone Akvan nears the coast
noticias.resumen: Cyclone Akvan, the third severe storm to hit India's east coast in a month, is expected to make landfall on November 20. Meanwhile, PM Modi led a meeting of his Council of Ministers.
noticias.texto:
India: Nearly 50,000 evacuated as Cyclone Akvan nears the coast
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Protests hit parts of Bangladesh ahead of Sheikh Hasina's return, Muhammad Yunus' ancestral home set ablaze
- Odisha evacuates about 50,000 as Cyclone Akvan, the third severe storm in a month, nears the coast
- Prime Minister Modi chairs meeting of high-level ministers to review governance initiatives
Here is a roundup of headlines from India from Thursday, November 19:
WATCH — India's online betting boom comes at a cost
Despite India's ban on online money games, betting platforms continue to attract players. For many, hopes of quick money turn into debt, addiction and financial ruin, leaving families to face devastating consequences.
Watch for more:
PM Modi chairs Council of Ministers’ meeting to review governance initiatives
Prime Minister Narendra Modi chaired a meeting of the Union Council of Ministers at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Wednesday, hours after returning from the Philippines.
"Council of ministers meeting since morning, extensive discussions on good governance initiatives," he wrote on social media.
Eleven secretaries, including those from the Home and Finance ministries, made presentations, according to local media. Topics included a recent World Bank report on India's progress in reducing extreme poverty, governance reforms, and welfare and youth schemes.
Modi sought feedback on targets set at the ministers' September "chintan shivir," or "brainstorming camp," where ministries were told to ensure 100% saturation of welfare schemes, Business Standard reported.
The meeting lasted about three and a half hours.
Wellington: Nicholls hundred drags New Zealand back after Bumrah’s early blows
Henry Nicholls made an unbeaten 113 to help New Zealand recover from 70-5 to finish the first day of the first Test at 243-5 in Wellington on Thursday. India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and chose to bowl.
Jasprit Bumrah, playing his first Test in about a year, bowled New Zealand captain Tom Latham with the third ball of the match. He finished with 3-52 from 17 overs, adding Daryl Mitchell and Tom Blundell.
Nicholls and Glenn Phillips then added an unbroken 173 after lunch as the pitch eased and India's other pacers lost their lines. Nicholls' 12th Test hundred came from 188 balls, 141 of them dot balls.
Devdutt Padikkal dropped him on 102. Phillips was 94 not out.
"You play at a venue like this and against a team like India, it's a special occasion," AFP cited Nicholls as saying.
India's batting coach, Sitanshu Kotak, said the team's less experienced bowlers could learn from how Bumrah adjusted to New Zealand conditions, AFP reported.
Bangladesh: Awami League lockdown turns violent ahead of Hasina's return, Yunus's ancestral home torched
Parts of Bangladesh shut down Thursday as police reported two members of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) were killed and the ancestral home of former interim leader Muhammad Yunus was set on fire.
The unrest comes ahead of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's planned return from exile in India next month, despite facing the death sentence there.
Her party, the Awami League, which was banned after Hasina was ousted, called for the nationwide "lockdown" after a week of protests over the government's rejection of her request for a new passport and identity card.
Police said two local BNP leaders were killed in Narail when Awami League activists attacked a BNP march, local media reported. It added that two other people, a local BNP leader and a transport worker, died in Faridpur and Pirojpur earlier this week.
Newspaper reports said suspected BNP activists attacked or set fire to the homes of two Awami League leaders in Dhaka.
Crude bombs went off in Dhaka before dawn and at least four people were wounded, the Press Trust of India reported. Reuters said 97 platoons of the Border Guard had been deployed across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur.
Authorities said flammable material was probably thrown into an unused ground-floor room of Yunus's Chattogram family home, and that relatives living upstairs were safe. At least 37 Grameen Bank branches and offices, which Yunus founded, have been targeted since November 10, the bank said.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said those behind the violence will be identified and prosecuted, and he accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting it. Awami League leaders could not be reached for comment, Reuters said.
Cyclone Akvan: Odisha evacuates thousands as severe storm nears the coast
Odisha has evacuated tens of thousands of people ahead of Cyclone Akvan, which is expected to cross the coast by noon Friday, the third severe cyclonic storm to threaten India's east coast in less than a month.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) expects landfall between Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh and Puri in Odisha with winds up to 110 kmph. The IMD now expects a severe cyclonic storm, not the very severe storm it projected earlier. Local media reported red alerts for heavy to extremely heavy rain in both states.
Reuters cited the chief minister's office, which said more than 47,000 people had been evacuated by Thursday. Local media put the figure at about 50,000 and said 3,000 cyclone shelters had been opened.
Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi said most evacuees were from Ganjam district. Schools in Ganjam, Gajapati, Puri, Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapara and Kandhamal are shut for three days from Thursday. Later, authorities announced that schools in Malkangiri, Rayagada and Koraput districts would also remain closed on Thursday and Friday.
"No evacuations in Andhra Pradesh yet," state disaster official Prakhar Jain told Reuters. "The storm has reduced in intensity."
Cyclone Arnab struck the region in late October and Cyclone Murasu earlier this month.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello!
This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest news from India, once again.
Odisha has announced school closures in multiple districts as Cyclone Akvan, the third severe storm to threaten India's east coast in a month, looks ready to make landfall.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi chaired a meeting with his Council of Ministers — his top team for governance at New Delhi's Bharat Mandapam.
Meanwhile, in neighboring Bangladesh, supporters of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina have called for a "lockdown" after days of protests. The ancestral home of former interim leader Muhammad Yunus was set on fire.
For this and more, follow our live blog.

noticias.titulo: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
noticias.resumen: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.
noticias.texto:
Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
November 19, 2026
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, is set to make its Nasdaq debut Thursday in one of the largest share sales in history.
The Claude maker offered 980 million shares at $83 (€76) per share, raising $81.3 billion. This values the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
This public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.
2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.
In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.
AI doubts trigger market turbulence
The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.
While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.
Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.
The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.
In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.
The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.
Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO
While OpenAI — the maker of ChatGPT — has delayed its public listing until next year, some analysts have been left scratching their heads at Anthropic's decision to proceed, even though the IPO is reportedly about six times oversubscribed.
"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.
Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.
"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."
Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.
"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."
Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive
Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.
In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.
"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."
AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'
Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction."
"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."
In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
Signs to watch, not reasons to flee
With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.
This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.
There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.
"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."
That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.
Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.
Is AI next in a long line of bubbles that burst?
In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.
When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.
Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.
"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.
Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18 and 19 to reflect the latest developments.

noticias.titulo: Crimean Bridge has been attacked again, Russian official says
noticias.resumen: The Crimean Bridge has been attacked again, Crimea's Russian-installed governor said. The attack comes as Vladimir Putin prepares to sit down with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping for joint talks in China.
noticias.texto:
Crimean Bridge has been attacked again, Russian official says
November 19, 2026
The Crimean Bridge was attacked for a third time this week, a Russian official said on Thursday.
Rail traffic had been temporarily suspended, according to Crimea's Russian-installed governor.
"The damage is currently being assessed," Sergei Aksyonov, the governor, initially said on Telegram, adding that emergency services were at the scene.
Aksyonov later announced that traffic was set to be restored starting from around 4 p.m. local time (1300 GMT).
TASS news agency reported it may take a few months for some sections of the bridge to become operational, citing Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin.
In an online post on Thursday, the Ukrainian military said that the attack had been carried out by its forces.
It stated that the strikes on Russian bridges hamper Moscow's ability to transport military supplies to the front line.
The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
Crimean Bridge attacked for a third time this week
This is the third Ukrainian attack this week targeting the strategic bridge that is a key symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
The bridge has played a key role in supplying Russian troops in occupied parts of southern Ukraine since the 2022 Russian invasion, making it a key target for Kyiv.
Steel arch of bridge collapses after Ukrainian drone strikes earlier this week
On Tuesday, Ukraine carried out a major attack on the bridge using missiles and drones, destroying the steel arch of the 19-kilometer-long road section of the crossing.
Ukraine's SBU security service had said that the "road span beneath it (the arch) has been completely destroyed."
The latest attack appears to have impacted rail traffic on the bridge, according to German press agency DPA.
The Ukrainian attack came just hours before an unprecedented meeting scheduled between Putin and his US and Chinese counterparts on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine's allies gather in Berlin for 'Coalition of the Willing' summit
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's European backers are convening in Berlin, with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also set to attend the meeting. Follow the latest.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine's allies attend 'Coalition of the Willing' summit in Berlin
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Ukraine's main European allies are convening in Berlin for 'Coalition of the Willing' talks
- Leaders of Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy are meeting at a time when President Donald Trump is set for talks with Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in China
- US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are also set to attend the meeting and will brief allies about discussions in China
Follow the latest on Thursday, 19th November, below:
Ukraine claims responsibility for third attack on Kerch bridge
The Ukrainian military on Thursday claimed responsibility for a strike on the Kerch Bridge.
The bridge was attacked on Wednesday for a third time this week, halting rail traffic briefly and damaging some sections.
In an online post, the Ukrainian military said that the strike had been carried out by its forces using Neptune coastal missiles.
It stated that the strikes on Russian bridges hamper Moscow's ability to transport military supplies to the front line.
The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
Prince Harry says he would return to military service to fight Russia if needed
The United Kingdom's Prince Harry said on Thursday he would rejoin the military to fight against Russia if needed.
"If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel," he said in an interview from Ukraine with The Telegraph.
"I think there's a lot that the whole world can learn from Ukraine," the prince said during an unannounced visit to the western city of Lviv over the weekend.
Prince Harry, a former British Army officer and the younger son of King Charles III, traveled to Ukraine for his fourth visit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, where he met with wounded veterans and medical staff.
"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, that doesn't mean that we're not at war," he told the UK newspaper.
He emphasized that "Ukraine are winning" and "there is no version where Russia is making any more advances"
Traffic set to resume on the damage Crimean bridge
Crimea's Russian-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said traffic was set to be restored on the attacked Kerch bridge starting from around 4 p.m. local time (1300 GMT) on Thursday.
TASS news agency reported it may take a few months for some sections of the bridge to become operational, citing Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin.
The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
Read DW's full report on the most recent Ukrainian attack on Kerch bridge.
Crimean Bridge comes under attack again, Russian official says
The Crimean Bridge was attacked for a third time this week, a Russian official said on Thursday.
Traffic had been temporarily suspended, according to Crimea's Russian-installed governor.
"The damage is currently being assessed," Sergei Aksyonov, the governor, said on Telegram, adding that emergency services were at the scene.
The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
UK to provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones
The UK pledged to provide Ukraine with long-range cruise missiles capable of reaching areas in Russia beyond the front lines.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to make that announcement at the "Coalition of the Willing" summit in Berlin.
The drones are a part of the support package for Kyiv worth £260 million pounds ($338 million, €311 million) ahead of the winter.
"Plunging millions of Ukrainians into the freezing cold and starving them of heat and warmth won’t see Putin win this war, it will only cement our resolve to support Ukraine," Burnham said, adding that he is "determined" to help Ukraine defend itself.
According to Burnham, Ukraine's backers are "as united as ever" to secure an end to the war with Russia.
'Coalition of the Willing' sends signal to Russia, Germany's Wadephul tells DW
German Foreign MinisterJohann Wadephul said the meeting of Ukraine's backers in Berlin should send a signal to Russia.
"It's really about time to be serious with the negotiations," Wadephul told DW.
According to Germany's top diplomat, Ukraine's allies are readying themselves for all possibilities, including the failure of negotiations, which would require supporting Kyiv's energy and food needs.
"We will also be on Ukraine's side militarily," he said.
'Coalition of the Willing' grouping is meeting in Berlin on Thursday
Germany's capital will host a meeting between a group of European leaders that support Ukrainein the war against Russia.
The meeting, dubbed the "Coalition of the Willing," includes German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will also be in attendance.
According to German officials, the meeting is intended to demonstrate the countries' commitment to legally binding security guarantees should a ceasefire agreement be reached between Russia and Ukraine.
The timing of the meeting is intended to allow the group to react quickly to announcements that come out of the meeting between US President Donald Trump ,Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping in China.
Trump might also meet Putin for a bilateral summit.
Welcome to our coverage
We'll be following updates from the so-called "Coalition of the Willing" meeting in Berlin.
The coalition is a grouping of countries that provide support to Ukraine against Russian aggression.
Leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy, as well as NATO head Mark Rutte, will attend the meeting today.
The show of support comes as Europe tries to forge a unified front in its attempt to be included in the US-led talks to end the war.
We'll have more from Germany's capital, thank you for joining.

noticias.titulo: Grand Theft Auto VI launches to global fanfare
noticias.resumen: After 13 years of waiting, fans around the world will get to play the latest installment in the blockbuster video game series. In focus: A tale of crime and violence in a fictionalized version of Miami.
noticias.texto:
Grand Theft Auto VI launches to global fanfare
November 19, 2026
Grand Theft Auto VI officially launched Thursday, ending a 13-year wait for one of the most anticipated games ever.
The game became playable at midnight local time, depending on location, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, meaning gamers in Asia will get to play the game ahead of users in the US and Europe.
In New Zealand, one of the first countries worldwide where the game became available, the release prompted internet providers to prepare for a spike in internet usage at midnight.
This is due to the game's size of 212 gigabytes, more than a quarter of the average New Zealand household's usage in a month.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA franchise, faces high expectationsn after 13 years of anticipation, with previous versions having become commercial and cultural hits around the world.
GTA games sold 470 million units worldwide, and the fifth installment generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days after its release in 2013.
GTA's global success
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar Games' parent company, saw its shares rise by more than eight percent the day before the game's release.
The game takes place in Vice City, a fictional version of Miami.
It follows Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple drawn into criminal networks while trying to secure a better life. GTA games are often criticized for including excessive violence and for glorifying crimes and drug use.
Lucia, a former prisoner, and Jason, an ex-military man, experience a series of criminal jobs that go wrong in the drug-trafficking world of Leonida, a fictional state based on Florida.
According to Rockstar, Leonida is the company's most detailed open world so far, extending beyond Vice City into smaller communities and nightlife hotspots inspired by locations in South Florida.
Music has been an intrinsic part of the GTA experience, and the latest game is expected to feature a soundtrack including artists like Tame Impala and SZA.

noticias.titulo: AI giant Anthropic raises more than $100 billion in record-setting IPO
noticias.resumen: Shares in the maker of the popular Claude artificial intelligence model will start trading on the Nasdaq Thursday.
noticias.texto:
AI giant Anthropic raises more than $100 billion in record-setting IPO
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Anthropic shares are about to make their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.
It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old artificial intelligence powerhouse, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.
Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.
The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
The total haul is more than $107 billion.
Anthropic valuation could rise or fall later on Thursday, when its shares start trading publicly on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.
The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.
A breakaway beginning
Anthropic's rise has been meteoric.
"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.
Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.
Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.
They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Opportunities and risks
The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.
"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.
"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."
There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.
"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"
Conflict with the Pentagon, and "pacing the frontier"
Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.
And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks. In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to "pace the frontier," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.
That essay followed a summer when AI agents from Anthropic's lab, as well as OpenAI and other competitors, were revealed to have hacked other companies, setting off a frenzy of concern about the risks of rogue agents. This week, California sued OpenAI over its agents that hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source software platform.
Anthropic's IPO prospectus dedicated dozens of pages to potential risks, including the possibility that people could lose control of AI, or that AI could take harmful actions on its own.
The company also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash. Indeed, the IPO comes just weeks after midterm elections in the United States, which analysts say likely herald a period of elevated scrutiny and oversight for AI firms. Data centers became a hot-button issue this election cycle, and tech stocks sank after the election as investors anticipated that the incoming Congress would crack down on the industry.
Still, Anthropic's prospectus was bullish about the development and spread of AI. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.
OpenAI had been on track to also list shares this year, but CEO Sam Altman postponed those plans, likely to next year, after the Hugging Face incident. At the Semafor conference on Monday Altman promised: "We will go public at some point."
"The world as a whole would like exposure to this," he continued. "And I think that's, you know, directionally a good thing to do."
Meanwhile, shares in SpaceX, the first of this year's AI mega-IPOs, are trading near their initial price of $135. After the company's June listing, the stock leapt to more than $200, then slid to as low as about $108 before recovering ground.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
