noticias.titulo: Geopolitics and genuine bonds: Negotiators on what it's like behind the scenes as COP tensions build
noticias.resumen: 'We're constantly surrounded by people and we sleep very little, five hours a night at most.'
noticias.texto:
'We're constantly surrounded by people and we sleep very little, five hours a night at most.'
The adrenaline and excitement are building behind the scenes at the UN climate talks in Türkiye, negotiators say, as envoys from nearly 200 nations clash over every word and comma ahead of hoped-for agreements on Friday (20 November).
Alliances are being built, AI is being wielded as negotiators from around the world navigate a melting pot of languages, and sneakers are the preferred footwear at the vast COP31 conference venue in Antalya, Türkiye.
"There's a crazy rush of adrenaline because we're in a real bubble of excitement. We're constantly surrounded by people and we sleep very little, five hours a night at most," Belgian negotiator Catherine Windey told news agency AFP.
"At the last two COPs, I ended up getting sick due to fatigue and the air conditioning in the negotiating rooms."
The annual talks aim to bring together countries to review, develop and implement major climate change agreements.
On Monday (16 November), co-host Australia unveiled the first draft of a broad political deal setting out sharply divergent positions on climate policy while calling for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels.
The sweeping 18-page proposal underscores the gulf that nearly 200 nations must bridge to reach consensus on Friday.
And the pace only intensifies as things progress – especially for smaller and poorer countries who are often those most impacted by climate change, and who are faced with the daunting task of rising above the clamour.
"It's exhausting, but we are here to ensure Africa's voice is heard," says Hamda Amin, a representative from Djibouti.
'Genuine emotional bonds are formed' at COP
As ever, alliances are key – and artificial intelligence is proving a crucial tool.
English is the language of COP, and negotiators who speak other languages are harnessing online translators.
The German development agency GIZ developed an AI-based tool called 'NegotiateCOP' to sift through voluminous documents, summarise them, and pinpoint potential allies who share their positions.
Personal ties matter enormously. Negotiators often come from their countries' climate ministries and are deeply committed to the cause.
"Genuine emotional bonds are formed," says Laurence Tubiana, one of the architects of the 2015 Paris COP.
'Geopolitics plays a huge role in the negotiations'
That year saw participating nations adopt the Paris Agreement to keep global warming "well below" 2°C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C to avert the worst impacts of global warming.
Expectations for this COP are more limited, with oil-producing nations such as Saudi Arabia opposing a phase-out of fossil fuels.
"Geopolitics plays a huge role in the negotiations. The atmosphere can be a bit disheartening, but there are pockets of hope," says the Belgian negotiator Windey.
She specialises in the process of supporting populations as they face the financial challenges of the ecological transition.
It is a specific field, and one in which the negotiators all know one another, she says – allowing for progress that may not be reflected in the final, official declarations, Windey argues.
"We can speak frankly during informal talks," she says.

noticias.titulo: Europe wants households ready for crises. But what if you can't prepare?
noticias.resumen: New EU guidelines urge citizens to manage the first 72 hours of an emergency independently. Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said it “has become an internationally recognised benchmark for household emergency preparedness.” Yet a University of Latvia survey found that only 8% feel prepared.
noticias.texto:
New EU guidelines urge citizens to manage the first 72 hours of an emergency independently. Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said it “has become an internationally recognised benchmark for household emergency preparedness.” Yet a University of Latvia survey found that only 8% feel prepared.
Food, water, and cash. Grab-and-go bags stocked with documents and medicines. Evacuation plans and practical skills, such as cooking without electricity and first aid.
This is how the European Commission’s new crisis guidelines advise citizens to be self-sufficient during the first 72 hours when cyber or drone attacks sabotage critical infrastructure and natural disasters disrupt transport and communication networks.
But few people are ready for a crisis breaking out today. The University of Latvia’s 2026 Baltic Individual Crisis Preparedness Barometer, which surveyed residents in 10 European cities across 8 Northern and Eastern EU countries (plus Iceland and Norway), found that just 8% feel quite or completely prepared. 44% plan to improve their preparedness within six months.
Preparedness today
Self-sufficiency during the first 72 hours of a crisis is crucial, as “it reduces the pressure on emergency services and allows them to focus on those most in need,” Hadja Lahbib, EU Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, told Euronews.
Yet the Baltic Individual Crisis Preparedness Barometer shows that at least half of residents in every surveyed city feel unprepared today. Dr. Ieva Birka, the Barometer's lead researcher, is not surprised. What surprises her is that nothing is changing.
“Preparedness has never been talked about more: there are national brochures, EU guidance and constant media coverage. Yet households’ actual material preparedness is not moving”, Birka explained.
Across the cities surveyed, only 31% have enough drinking water at home and 25% at work to last 72 hours or more. 50% think they have enough cash, and 71% believe they have enough food. While 73% have first-aid supplies, only 38% have a battery-powered AM/FM radio.
Differences between cities largely reflect how close people feel an attack is, Birka said. Vilnius is the only capital where the unprepared are a minority, as 67% consider an attack a major threat. But “feeling closer to the threat doesn’t mean being stocked up. Even in Vilnius, only about a quarter of respondents had three days’ worth of water,” she added.
Many people can’t afford
“Being prepared does not have to be expensive”, said Lahbib, suggesting that simple steps, including strong social networks and essentials such as food, water and a torch, can be real game-changers.
But many people can’t afford to be prepared. A family of four needs 36 litres of water for three days, non-perishable food, a battery-powered radio, first-aid supplies, medicines and cash. These essentials cost about €100–150 in Baltic capitals, while a fully stocked crisis kit with sleeping bags and tents can exceed €300, Birka explained. If heating fails, “unless you have a fireplace, the alternatives are generators or portable power stations, which cost hundreds of euros more”, she added.
About 30% of respondents say they need financial help to prepare. “Support should be targeted rather than universal,” Birka said, suggesting vouchers or ready-made kits for low-income households, distributed through municipalities and social services.
Asked whether the EU could fund preparedness, Lahbib said the Commission has launched “a behavioural study to better understand preparedness levels among low-income groups”. The results are expected next year.
When your preparedness depends on others
Money is not the only constraint. A 2026 European Disability Forum report, citing UN data, finds that 91% of people with disabilities in Europe lack a personal disaster plan, and 43% can’t evacuate without help. Accessible early warning systems cut the number to 22%, yet just 10% receive risk information in accessible formats like braille or sign language.
While the survey doesn’t include data specifically on people with disabilities or those who rely on assistive devices, Birka thinks “it's important to remember that for these groups, self-sufficiency depends on other people, so carers need to be prepared themselves.”
The Commission urges inclusive, accessible evacuations, transport, and shelters that meet diverse needs, with people with disabilities involved in planning. First-aid responders should be trained to communicate effectively, identify needs, and provide targeted support.
Birka wants these measures included in national and municipal emergency plans, not as "an optional extra”. She advises on personal emergency plans and support networks, voluntary registers of people who need assistance, backup power for medical and assistive devices, and accessible evacuation.
Preparedness is also psychological
For others, the issue is psychological. In Vilnius, where people feel the threat most heavily, 42% say the main obstacle is the psychological difficulty of thinking about it.
“More leaflets won’t close the gap,” Birka said, stressing that simply giving citizens more information about preparedness won't solve the problem. “People want more direct reassurance from governments that there is a plan, that crises will be handled, and that if individuals do their share in preparing, the country, civil protection and emergency services, and the army will do theirs”, she explained.
Practical help is what makes the difference. For Birka, this includes concrete action plans and raising awareness in their own neighbourhoods. Formats should suit the audience, from short videos for younger generations to printed materials for older audiences.
Same guidelines, different levels of preparedness
The guidelines are non-binding. “Member States have been involved throughout,” Lahbib said, but “the EU cannot guarantee that citizens are ‘equally prepared’. That is the responsibility of each Member State.”
This could leave Europeans unevenly prepared and widen the existing gap between member states. Birka argued that consistently tracking progress across countries and over time can show whether national governments are taking the EU’s advice seriously.
The lead researcher urged the EU to adopt shared indicators and conduct regular, comparable surveys with clear, measurable targets, for example, tracking how many households have enough water for three days. “Shared standards for measuring and reporting would make progress visible and create healthy pressure to act”, said Birka.

noticias.titulo: North Korea expanding original uranium enrichment facility, UN nuclear watchdog says
noticias.resumen: The IAEA has not had access to Yongbyon or other locations in North Korea since the country kicked out the agency’s inspectors in 2009.
noticias.texto:
The IAEA has not had access to Yongbyon or other locations in North Korea since the country kicked out the agency’s inspectors in 2009.
North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex, the head of the UN nuclear watchdog said, in yet another sign that Pyongyang is delivering on its vow to bolster its nuclear weapons programme.
The assessment by International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi came as US President Donald Trump expressed his eagerness to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un while he is in Asia for a summit in China.
“Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late-October 2026,” Grossi said in a statement to the IAEA’s board of governors.
“The ongoing expansion of the DPRK’s uranium enrichment program remains a cause for serious concern.”
DPRK stands for Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
The IAEA has not had access to Yongbyon or other locations in North Korea since the country kicked out the agency’s inspectors in 2009.
The IAEA has said it uses satellite imagery and open source information to monitor developments in the North’s nuclear programme.
North Korea has called its Yongbyon complex “the heart” of its nuclear programme.
Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon.
Observers say North Korea has taken steps to build additional uranium enrichment facilities at Yongbyon and elsewhere since Kim’s earlier high-stakes nuclear diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019.
Last year, South Korea’s Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.
While Trump expressed interest in meeting with Kim, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said no meeting was yet scheduled for Trump’s visit to China but said the president is prepared to begin a new dialogue with Pyongyang.
North Korea hasn’t responded to Trump’s fresh overtures.
Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the US drops its “hostile policy” against his country and respects what he calls the North’s status as a nuclear state.
Experts say North Korea is eager to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that it could demand the lifting of UN economic sanctions.

noticias.titulo: Chronically online? ‘Problematic internet use’ is a growing global health concern, experts warn
noticias.resumen: Experts called for stricter regulation of digital platforms, warning that features designed to keep users online can fuel harmful internet use.
noticias.texto:
Experts called for stricter regulation of digital platforms, warning that features designed to keep users online can fuel harmful internet use.
“Problematic” internet use has emerged as a major global public health concern, potentially affecting more than 10% of the world’s population and taking a substantial societal toll, experts warned.
Problematic usage of the internet (PUI) covers a wide range of behaviours, including gambling, gaming, pornography consumption, social media use and online shopping. These activities are not inherently harmful, but they are considered “problematic” when they interfere with daily life or rise to the level of a medical disorder, for example, gambling addiction.
In a report published in The Lancet Psychiatry, experts in public health, psychology and policy argued that governments should recognise PUI as a global public health concern and regulate the design features that keep people online, such as infinite scroll and autoplay.
“From a public health perspective, although many PUI- related behaviours might not reach the thresholds for clinical diagnosis, taken together, they constitute a substantial public health problem,” the authors wrote.
People with problematic internet use often also have mental health conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), sleep disturbances, eating disorders, self-harm and suicidal ideation or attempts, the report said.
The report also linked PUI with interpersonal conflict, loneliness, family dysfunction, lower academic and work productivity and burnout.
Young people, those in low- and middle-income countries and people with mental health disorders appeared to be most at risk. It’s not clear whether PUI is becoming more common or if the consequences are simply becoming better understood.
Platform design increases the risk
While gambling, gaming and pornography existed long before the internet, the authors warned that digital platforms make these indulgences constantly accessible and have features that can make them addictive, such as algorithmic precision and real-time feedback.
Loneliness, poor family relations and spending more time online could all contribute to harmful behaviours.
However, the report said PUI could not be explained solely by individual vulnerabilities and was also shaped or amplified by the specific design features of online platforms and services, for example, social media algorithms.
Research on the issue is still underway, but the authors said there is enough evidence to justify a “precautionary approach” in public policy. They called for an internationally coordinated approach to address harms from PUI.
Current policy approaches may be insufficient. Social media bans that focus on age limits, for example, do not necessarily address the features that encourage compulsive internet use, such as infinite scrolls and push notifications, the report noted.
The authors argued that responsibility should lie with online platforms, not with individual users, and recommended holding those products to the same safety standards as tobacco, alcohol and gambling.
The report called for a range of actions, including restricting high-risk features, independent auditing of algorithms and binding rules on age limits and marketing restrictions.
The researchers urged governments to move away from voluntary industry self-regulation and towards enforceable standards that would make safety features the default and curb features designed to maximize engagement.
“The goal should be to prioritise public health over industry interests to reduce the societal harms of PUI,” the authors concluded.

noticias.titulo: Europe must make the EU–UK Security and Defence Partnership work
noticias.resumen: 'Europe’s security environment will not wait for perfect alignment. Our leaders should seize the opportunities within reach. Our industry needs them to do so,' write Micael Johansson and David Lockwood, senior representatives of the European aerospace, security and defence industries, in an op-ed.
noticias.texto:
'Europe’s security environment will not wait for perfect alignment. Our leaders should seize the opportunities within reach. Our industry needs them to do so,' write Micael Johansson and David Lockwood, senior representatives of the European aerospace, security and defence industries, in an op-ed.
When EU and UK leaders meet at their summit tomorrow, the temptation will be to take comfort in improved relations. Amid war in Europe, intensifying great-power competition and mounting pressure on industrial capacity, better relations must now translate into very concrete results.
The EU–UK Security and Defence Partnership agreed last year was an important step, recognising that Europe’s security challenges are best addressed through closer EU–UK cooperation. Political recognition is useful. The task now is to build on it with greater urgency.
The EU and the UK share decades of industrial integration
In modern Europe, power begins as much in factories, laboratories and assembly lines as in ministries. EU Member States and the UK share decades of industrial integration: common standards; integrated supply chains; research, operational and regulatory cooperation; and long-established relationships of trust.
This applies to civil aeronautics and defence alike. Aerospace, defence and security companies on both sides of the Channel form an industrial ecosystem spanning flight technologies, ground and naval platforms, advanced manufacturing, electronics, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and digital technologies. Decarbonising European aviation requires a strong, integrated European research and industrial base. Every major European aircraft carries UK technology, while UK aerospace depends on EU supply chains and access to the EU Single Market.
UK industry is woven into the fabric of European capability, just as EU industry is embedded in the UK. Geography, capability and integration make the UK the EU’s closest and most natural industrial partner.
Both sides must make pragmatic decisions
A more integrated EU–UK approach would immediately deliver speed, scale and efficiency at a time when these qualities are increasingly decisive. It could strengthen security of supply, reduce duplication, enhance interoperability, support collaborative research and long-term capability development. This requires closer industrial planning, research and innovation cooperation, pragmatic alignment on standards and certification, and common principles for applying open modular system architecture of platforms and solutions.
This is not about revisiting past political debates or one side accommodating the other. It is about aligning Europe’s aerospace, defence and security capacity with a more demanding strategic environment.
The responsibility is shared. The EU has ambitious goals for aerospace innovation, defence readiness and industrial capacity. The UK has signalled its commitment to European security and closer cooperation. Both sides must make pragmatic decisions if those ambitions are to translate into tangible outcomes.
UK participation in selected EU defence initiatives could be enabled
A dedicated industrial cooperation framework could enable UK participation in selected EU defence initiatives — under fair conditions and with an appropriate UK financial contribution — where this strengthens readiness, industrial capacity, supply-chain resilience and interoperability.
This should include possible UK participation in relevant European Competitiveness Fund activities, under mutually agreed conditions and with an appropriate financial contribution. Such participation would build on the longstanding integration of the UK within Europe’s aerospace, defence and security industrial base and support closer EU–UK industrial cooperation.
A further step would be for the UK to sign an Administrative Arrangement with the European Defence Agency (EDA). An established mechanism already exists to support cooperation with third countries, including Norway, Switzerland, Ukraine and the United States. Extending it to the UK would enable participation in selected EDA activities and programmes, strengthen dialogue within the EU-UK Security and Defence Partnership, and support interoperability.
Should the European Security Council be established and include the UK, it could provide a useful platform for closer cooperation, particularly if it integrates industrial and technological cooperation alongside the broader security agenda.
The UK should provide access to UK programmes and procurement
The UK, in turn, should provide reciprocal access for EU industry to UK programmes and procurement; sustain regulatory alignment in airworthiness certification, export controls and defence-relevant standards.
The EU and the UK do not need to agree on everything to make progress. Practical cooperation can build trust and momentum and demonstrate the value of working together. Pursuing perfect alignment from the outset risks delaying vital outcomes that would benefit both sides today.
That will require strategic maturity from both sides: a focus on effectiveness and existing strengths and a political choice acknowledging the relationship’s unique nature. Europe can choose to develop its industrial base while reducing its dependency on non-European suppliers, or to invest time in narrower constructions that may deliver more slowly.
The EU and the UK should move from agreement to delivery
A coherent EU–UK industrial partnership would strengthen competitiveness, innovation, technological leadership and Europe’s capacity to operate at scale in civil aviation and defence alike.
It would also strengthen NATO’s European pillar by better aligning industrial capability with operational needs. More balanced burden-sharing requires a strong European industry capable of delivering the full spectrum of capabilities needed for transatlantic security, drawing on strengths on both sides of the Channel.
It would demonstrate that the EU-UK partnership is more than a diplomatic formality, and that shared interests can be translated into practical benefits for the whole European community.
The foundations are in place. The strategic rationale is clear. The opportunity to build on this uniquely integrated relationship is real. What remains is the political choice.
The forthcoming summit should be the moment when the EU and the UK move from agreement to delivery. Europe’s security environment will not wait for perfect alignment. Our leaders should seize the opportunities within reach. Our industry needs them to do so.
ASD is the Aerospace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe. Its overall representation adds up to more than 4,000 companies, accounting for 99% of industry’s total turnover and 94% of its total employment in Europe.
ADS is the UK trade association for the aerospace, defence, security and space sectors, representing almost 1,500 businesses. It enables prosperity, clean growth, and aims to secure advanced manufacturing’s collective advantage. ADS is a member of ASD.

noticias.titulo: Ho ho homework: London's Santa School prepares Father Christmas performers for the festive season
noticias.resumen: Professional Santas are heading back to school in South London to prepare for the Christmas season.Training includes everything from sign language and the latest toy trends to handling difficult questions from children.
noticias.texto:
Professional Santas are heading back to the classroom in South London, in preparation for the busy Christmas season at the Ministry of Fun's Santa School.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
Now in its 28th year, the training covers everything from learning sign language and keeping up with the latest toy trends to handling some of the more difficult questions children might ask.
For Santa trainer Matt Grist, the role comes with a serious responsibility: "In order to deliver an encounter that is magical, you have to take it seriously, and you have to really care about the encounter that you have with the child and about the content. It's a duty we have, really. It's an obligation we have," he says.

noticias.titulo: Leaders of US, China and Russia hold historic trilateral summit
noticias.resumen: Trump declared that “we have great responsibilities to solve problems that affect the entire planet,” as he joined China's Xi and Russia’s Putin for the historic trilateral summit in China, while Xi said “the world is at peace when great powers live in harmony.” The meeting ended without statements.
noticias.texto:
Trump declared that “we have great responsibilities to solve problems that affect the entire planet,” as he joined China's Xi and Russia’s Putin for the historic trilateral summit in China, while Xi said “the world is at peace when great powers live in harmony.” The meeting ended without statements.
The unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen between US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin ended on Thursday without statements from the three leaders, after Trump declared at the beginning that the three global powers "are making history".
Opening their first such summit, which could be a pivotal moment in world history, Trump said the three leaders “will talk about all problems that are being discussed in the world.”
“We have great responsibilities to solve problems that affect the entire planet," he added.
Trump said he had a "long discussion" with Putin on Russia's ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and that all sides "would like to see an end to that war".
Xi joined Trump in saying their summit “has groundbreaking significance”, adding that “the world is at peace when great powers live in harmony," calling on the three countries to “abandon Cold War mentality, not pursue decoupling and breaking chains”.
"The three countries should work together to address global challenges,” and that they "can strengthen coordination to safeguard global energy supply chain stability," Xi said. “Adversity reveals true responsibility.”
Putin said that Russia’s war in Ukraine would be part of the talks, stating that “we have shared interests in Ukraine.”
“Russia, the US and China are united not only by their status as victorious nations in World War II, but also by their responsibility for maintaining international peace,” Putin said.
However, after the summit ended, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Russian media that Ukraine was not "the central topic" at the summit.
Just as the summit was starting, China's state news agency published a statement from Xi saying that “nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world.”
In his opening statements, Trump said that the “three countries are uniquely positioned to discuss nuclear weapons."
“Too often past leaders avoided talking to leaders they had disagreements with,” Trump added.
The leaders posed for a family photo without shaking hands as they started their summit and made no statements when it concluded.
The meeting ended after around an hour and 20 minutes. Trump left the venue immediately for Shenzhen's airport and took off shortly after, while Xi accompanied Putin who also departed for Russia.
China's state news agency Xinhua published the full text of what it called the "trilateral peace declaration," listing four key points: commitment to UN reform, plans to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, respect for the immunity of state officials and opposition to the ICC and similar institutions abusing their jurisdiction, as well as an agreement to hold dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and non-proliferation.
The declaration makes no explicit reference to Ukraine, Iran, Taiwan or North Korea.
High-stakes bilateral talks before the trilateral
The US and Chinese presidents met bilaterally earlier on Thursday in their third substantial meeting this year.
During the meeting, Trump said that the US and China want to help end the war in Ukraine, stating that "we're looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine."
The US president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a key site of attacks in the Iran war.
Xi said that relations between the US and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi said.
Trump also met Putin ahead of the trilateral, stating that “we’ve had a great relationship for many years.”
Their meeting marks the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia's all-out war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start,” Trump said as he greeted Putin, saying "Who is he? He's my friend."
The summit has stoked fears that the three powerful men may seek to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by making decisions impacting the fate of Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv or Europe.
A wider debate was raging among observers on social media over whether the summit can be dubbed a "Yalta 2.0," while others claim it should rather be dubbed Munich 1938, given the fundamental differences in time, space and the protagonists.
To underline the weight of the summit and balance the focus of European and wider Western media, Asian television stations and newspapers were focusing on the possible consequences for their own countries.
Chinese state media, particularly Xinhua and People's Daily, framed the APEC summit and the trilateral around Xi's diplomatic leadership, multilateral cooperation and China's commitment to free trade. Beijing is presenting the trilateral summit as an opportunity to promote global peace and strategic stability among major powers.
In the South Korean media, the recurring theme was concern over a potential “Yalta 2.0” conference, in which the leaders could discuss the future of the Korean peninsula without Seoul's participation, with news agency Yonhap reporting that the South Korean government has conveyed these concerns to both Washington and Beijing.
The coverage is also focusing on the possibility of renewed US–North Korea dialogue and the risk of tacit acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status.
Japanese media are focusing on strained Sino-Japanese relations, with one major TV channel reporting on the first face-to-face encounter between Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Xi in about a year.
No formal bilateral meeting between Takaichi and Xi has been scheduled, and the Japanese media reported that Takaichi was seeking a discussion with Trump following the trilateral summit.
Germany was also due to host Ukraine's allies for a "Coalition of the Willing" meeting on Thursday involving US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.

noticias.titulo: France: Hundreds raise a glass to Beaujolais Nouveau in Lyon
noticias.resumen: Lyon welcomed the arrival of Beaujolais Nouveau with a lively nighttime parade of wine barrels, flaming torches and brass music. Hundreds gathered to celebrate the first tastings of this year's wine.
noticias.texto:
Flaming torches, blaring trumpets and wooden casks rolled down cobbles or carted on tractors set Lyon’s thoroughfares abuzz as costumed revellers led the city's annual wine parade. Drawing dense crowds, the festivities peaked with the theatrical uncorking of the season’s first bottles on stage, sparking music, dancing and cheers as the inaugural glasses were handed out.
Hailing from the hills just north of Lyon, Beaujolais Nouveau hits the shelves just weeks after the grapes are picked, sustaining a quintessential French autumn ritual. Celebrated globally on the third Thursday of November, the event heralds the exact stroke at which the new vintage may legally be sold — a light, fruit-forward wine meant for immediate enjoyment rather than long ageing.
What began as a local harvest marker is now a lively tribute to French winemaking heritage, bringing producers and townspeople shoulder to shoulder. Through its torchlit march and midnight pouring, Lyon once again turned the launch into an exuberant street festival.

noticias.titulo: Rare stonefly found beside vanishing glacier on Chile's Navarino Island
noticias.resumen: An international team of scientists, including researchers from the University of Barcelona, has discovered a rare insect beside the remnants of a glacier in Chilean Patagonia.
noticias.texto:
An international team of scientists, including researchers from the University of Barcelona, has discovered a rare insect beside the remnants of a glacier in Chilean Patagonia.
At the southern tip of Chilean Patagonia, near Cape Horn, the last remnants of a glacier have been the scene of an unexpected discovery. A group of scientists has found a rare insect on Navarino Island, a region where the ice is retreating and exposing a landscape that is constantly changing.
The discovery is presented in a study published in November 2026 in the scientific journal "Ecology (source in Spanish)", which examines ice loss in this area and documents the presence of the insect. It is a stonefly, a type of insect closely linked to freshwater ecosystems. It belongs to the Gripopterygidae family, found in different regions of the southern hemisphere.
The researchers have not been able to identify it among known species, which raises the possibility that it is a species not yet described by science. However, further studies will be needed to confirm this.
A discovery amid the thaw
The find took place next to the remnants of a glacier on Navarino Island, in the Tierra del Fuego archipelago, an area where ice loss is changing environmental conditions. Glaciers are not only part of the landscape. The water from their melt feeds nearby ecosystems and creates particular conditions for numerous organisms. When the ice disappears, these environments change as well.
For now, it is not known whether the insect lives exclusively in this area or whether it is also present in other parts of Patagonia. The study, titled "Rapid ice loss and a rare stonefly from Chile's southernmost glacier remnants" ("Rápida pérdida de hielo y un extraño plecóptero en los últimos vestigios glaciares del extremo sur de Chile", in Spanish), has not determined its conservation status either.
The research, led by Javier Rendoll-Cárcamo, involves scientists linked to institutions such as the University of Magallanes, the University of Barcelona and the British Antarctic Survey.
The study was led from the Cabo de Hornos International Centre (CHIC), based in Puerto Williams, where Javier Rendoll-Cárcamo works as a postdoctoral researcher, together with the Millennium Institute BASE and the University of Magallanes. CHIC also funded the research.

noticias.titulo: The dark side of AI: US data centres emit more carbon than all of Denmark
noticias.resumen: The Harvard study has revealed that pledges alone might not be enough, even as COP31 negotiators push for cleaner energy use in data centres.
noticias.texto:
The Harvard study has revealed that pledges alone might not be enough, even as COP31 negotiators push for cleaner energy use in data centres.
For years, activists and experts have warned about the environmental impact of data centres. Now, a Harvard study has put an eye-opening figure on their carbon footprint.
According to researchers at the Ivy League university, the electricity consumed by 403 of the largest data centres in the US over one year generated about as much CO2 as Denmark – a country with a population of just six million.
In one of the first studies to estimate the electricity consumption and emissions of hyperscale data centres since the rise of AI, the researchers estimated their electricity consumption produced 25.7 million tonnes of CO2 between May 2024 and April 2025.
This is about two to three times higher than an earlier estimate based on 2018 data. More than half the power came from planet-warming fossil fuels, too – mostly natural gas and coal.
“We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions,” Francesca Dominici, a Harvard biostatistics professor, told news agency AP.
The study comes just as COP31 negotiators launch a voluntary pledge, calling on data centre operators to use cleaner energy and disclose their environmental impact.
All the while, Europe is building up for its own data centre boom, too.
Europe’s data centre boom is underway
Within the next seven years, the EU wants to triple its data centre capacity as it seeks to compete in the global AI race. The building boom is already beginning. Property consultancy CBRE expects European capacity to grow by 20 per cent in 2026 alone.
While cities like London, Frankfurt and Paris have already become major hubs, electricity shortages have forced others – including Amsterdam and Dublin – to pause some new developments, prompting investors to look elsewhere to fill the void.
In Finland, 145 data centre projects have been announced nationwide in recent years – 60 this year alone. More than 50 are in the pipeline in Spain as well, 17 of which are already under construction.
Italy is attracting developers, too. In Puglia, local authorities have received 29 requests for electricity grid connections for potential data centres, while CBRE reports that Milan is expected to overtake Dublin as Europe’s fifth-largest data centre market by 2028.
Data centre construction comes at a cost
The IEA estimates data centres will account for 10 per cent of additional electricity demand in the EU by 2030, putting a strain on its aging power grids.
Residents have also raised major concerns about water consumption, noise pollution and the amount of land being given over to data centres – among other fears.
In July, the UK government overruled a local council to approve a €585 million plan to convert the former Truman Brewery in east London into a mixed-use development, including shops, offices, homes and a data centre.
Campaigners took to the streets in protest, saying the data centre alone could consume as much electricity as 15,000 homes. But the project would create just 44 new homes – and only six for social housing.
In October, more than 1,000 people representing about 40 local committees gathered in Milan to protest Italy’s data centre expansion and demand a halt to new developments.
Less than a month later, activists broke into a Microsoft construction site in Amsterdam, climbing a crane, setting off flares and clashing with police.
Then, in November, Stop Dirty Data Centres – a coalition of more than 100 environmental, digital rights and community groups – organised demonstrations in 15 countries to demand a freeze on new data centres until governments address their impact on utility bills, housing and resources.
How Europe plans to reduce the environmental impact
The Harvard researchers found that a data centre’s footprint largely depends on where it is built. For example, the same amount of electricity generated more than twice as much carbon in the state of Wyoming, where the power mostly comes from coal, than in Oregon, where hydropower is a sizable part of the energy mix.
They also found that operators rarely disclose their electricity consumption, making it difficult to calculate their emissions individually.
The EU hopes to avoid similar stumbling blocks.
Under the Energy Efficiency Directive, data centres using at least 500 kilowatts of computing power must report their energy and water consumption.
In September, the European Commission proposed A-to-G ratings for energy and water efficiency, similar to what is used to label household appliances.
Some operators claim to be finding ways to reduce their impact, too.
In Portugal, for example, Start Campus is developing a 1.2-gigawatt data centre complex in Sinesthat uses seawater for cooling. And in Helsinki, the city’s municipal energy company plans to recover enough excess heat from a new data centre to keep about 70,000 apartments warm annually once it is fully operational.
